cards.title: The prince who saw old age
cards.text: According to tradition, Prince Siddhartha grew up shielded from suffering. Venturing outside the palace, he finally saw an old man, a sick man and a corpse, then a calm wandering ascetic. Shaken, he left home to find out whether a life could be free of suffering.
cards.author: Siddhartha Gautama (the Buddha)
cards.source: The legend of the Four Sights, from traditional biographies of the Buddha
cards.more:
Siddhartha Gautama lived in what is now Nepal and northern India, probably around the 5th century BC, though scholars disagree on the exact dates. The story of the four sights is legend, but it captures the question Buddhism starts with: if ageing, illness and death come to everyone, how should we live?

After years of extreme self-denial that nearly killed him, he is said to have found a middle way and reached awakening while meditating under a tree. ‘Buddha’ simply means ‘awakened one’. This thread walks through what he taught, one idea at a time, starting from that first honest look at suffering.

thread.title: Buddhism in 7 cards

cards.title: A diagnosis in four steps
cards.text: The Buddha’s first teaching is shaped like a doctor’s diagnosis. Life involves dukkha: suffering, unease, the sense that things never quite satisfy. It has a cause: craving. It can end. And there is a path that leads to its ending.
cards.author: Siddhartha Gautama (the Buddha)
cards.source: Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11)
cards.more:
These are the Four Noble Truths, said to be the subject of the Buddha’s first sermon, given to five former companions in a deer park at Sarnath, near Varanasi. Dukkha is often translated as suffering, but it’s broader: the stress of wanting things to be other than they are, the background itch of dissatisfaction even when life is going fine.

The structure matters as much as the content. Name the problem honestly, find its cause, trust that a cure is possible, then follow a treatment. It’s a practical, almost clinical approach to the human condition. The next cards unpack each step, starting with the cause.

thread.title: Buddhism in 7 cards

cards.text: The thirst of a thoughtless man grows like a creeper; he runs from life to life, like a monkey seeking fruit in the forest.
cards.author: The Buddha
cards.source: Dhammapada, verse 334 (trans. F. Max Müller, 1881)
cards.more:
The second truth names the cause of suffering: taṇhā, which literally means ‘thirst’, and Müller keeps that image. Craving isn’t just wanting things; it’s a restless reaching that never settles. Get the fruit, and your hand is already moving to the next branch.

The Buddha didn’t say that wanting food or love is evil. The trouble is clinging: needing things to be a certain way, and suffering when they aren’t. You can see it in miniature in any phone session: one more scroll, one more check. Next time you reach for something, pause and notice the reaching itself. That noticing is where practice begins.

thread.title: Buddhism in 7 cards

cards.text: ‘All created things perish,’ he who knows and sees this becomes passive in pain; this is the way to purity.
cards.author: The Buddha
cards.source: Dhammapada, verse 277 (trans. F. Max Müller, 1881)
cards.more:
This verse states the first of the three marks of existence: impermanence. Everything that arises from causes, from moods to mountains to relationships, eventually passes. Müller’s phrase ‘passive in pain’ means something like ‘no longer pushed around by suffering’.

Why would seeing impermanence help? Because so much pain comes from treating changing things as if they were permanent: expecting a good moment to last forever, or a bad one never to end. Seeing clearly that both will pass makes it easier to enjoy the first without grasping and get through the second without despair. Try noticing one thing today that has already changed.

thread.title: Buddhism in 7 cards

cards.title: Look for the self in charge
cards.text: The Buddha asked his listeners to examine their body, feelings, perceptions, mental habits and consciousness. Each one changes, and none is fully under our control. So which of them is a permanent self? None, he argued. This is anattā, not-self.
cards.author: Siddhartha Gautama (the Buddha)
cards.source: Anattalakkhana Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 22.59)
cards.more:
This is traditionally the Buddha’s second sermon, and it holds his hardest and most misunderstood idea. He wasn’t saying you don’t exist. He was saying that what you call ‘me’ is a process, a flowing bundle of changing parts, not a fixed thing hidden behind them.

It connects directly to the earlier cards. If craving causes suffering, a lot of that craving is about protecting and enlarging this imagined fixed self: its image, its status, its need to be right. Loosening that grip can feel surprisingly light. Next time your pride is stung, ask yourself what exactly is being hurt.

thread.title: Buddhism in 7 cards

cards.title: The middle way out
cards.text: Having tried both palace luxury and near-starvation, the Buddha rejected both extremes. His fourth truth is a middle path with eight parts: right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration. It’s less a list of rules than a training in wisdom, ethics and attention.
cards.author: Siddhartha Gautama (the Buddha)
cards.source: Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11)
cards.more:
The eight parts are traditionally grouped into three areas. Wisdom covers view and intention: seeing how things are and meaning well. Ethics covers speech, action and livelihood: how you treat others and earn your living. Meditation covers effort, mindfulness and concentration: training the mind itself.

‘Right’ here means something like skilful, not obedient. The parts work together like the spokes of a wheel, which is why an eight-spoked wheel became a symbol of Buddhism. The middle way also works as everyday advice. When you keep swinging between extremes, the answer is often a steady, sustainable practice somewhere in between.

thread.title: Buddhism in 7 cards

cards.text: All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts. If a man speaks or acts with an evil thought, pain follows him, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the carriage.
cards.author: The Buddha
cards.source: Dhammapada, verse 1 (trans. F. Max Müller, 1881)
cards.more:
The Dhammapada, a collection of verses from the early Buddhist canon, opens with this line, and it makes a fitting end to this thread. Suffering, craving, impermanence and the illusion of a fixed self all have to be worked with through the mind, and the mind can be trained.

The next verse completes the pair: act with a pure thought, and happiness follows like a shadow that never leaves. That isn’t magical thinking. It’s a claim about cause and effect: habits of attention and intention shape what we experience. Start small. Catch one unkind or anxious thought today, and choose what to do with it.

thread.title: Buddhism in 7 cards

cards.text: The thirty spokes unite in the one nave; but it is on the empty space (for the axle), that the use of the wheel depends. Clay is fashioned into vessels; but it is on their empty hollowness, that their use depends.
cards.author: Laozi
cards.source: Tao Teh King, chapter 11 (trans. James Legge, 1891)
cards.more:
This short chapter of the Tao Te Ching goes on to doors and windows: a room is useful because of the space they cut out of the walls. Laozi’s point is that what isn’t there matters as much as what is. We notice the solid parts of things and overlook the emptiness that makes them work.

It’s a handy lens for a crowded life. A calendar with no gaps can’t take anything new. A conversation with no pauses leaves no room to listen. A page with no white space is hard to read. Try protecting one empty hour this week, and see what it makes possible.

cards.text: The tree which fills the arms grew from the tiniest sprout; the tower of nine storeys rose from a (small) heap of earth; the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step.
cards.author: Laozi
cards.source: Tao Teh King, chapter 64 (trans. James Legge, 1891)
cards.more:
This is the source of a line you’ve probably seen as ‘a journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step’. A li is a traditional Chinese measure of distance, historically about a third of a mile. The chapter is about handling things while they are small: problems are easiest to solve early, and great things grow from humble starts.

The motivational reading is fine, but Laozi’s emphasis is subtler. Pay attention to the small and the early, because that’s where outcomes are decided. Tiny habits, small kindnesses and minor warning signs all count. Big results are mostly made of little moments nobody noticed.

cards.text: Yu, shall I teach you what knowledge is? When you know a thing, to hold that you know it; and when you do not know a thing, to allow that you do not know it;—this is knowledge.
cards.author: Confucius
cards.source: Analects, Book 2.17 (trans. James Legge, 1861)
cards.more:
Yu was Zilu, one of Confucius’ most loyal and most impulsive disciples. The Analects is a collection of short sayings and conversations recorded by Confucius’ followers, and this one reads like a gentle correction for a student who liked to sound certain.

Confucius’ point is that knowing where your knowledge ends is itself knowledge, maybe the most useful kind. Pretending to know shuts learning down; admitting you don’t opens it up. Socrates made a strikingly similar point in Athens a few generations later. Try saying ‘I don’t know’ once this week in a moment where you would normally bluff.

cards.text: When I walk along with two others, they may serve me as my teachers. I will select their good qualities and follow them, their bad qualities and avoid them.
cards.author: Confucius
cards.source: Analects, Book 7.21 (trans. James Legge, 1861)
cards.more:
Confucius was famous as a teacher, yet he described himself first as a learner. In his view, every companion is a lesson. Someone with a good quality shows you something to copy; someone with a bad one shows you something to avoid, and maybe something to look for in yourself.

This makes learning available everywhere, not just in books or classrooms. A rude stranger, a generous colleague and a patient friend are all teaching, if you pay attention. Elsewhere in the Analects he says that when you see someone falling short, you should turn inward and examine yourself. Treat the next three people you talk to as teachers.

cards.text: A good cook changes his chopper once a year,—because he cuts. An ordinary cook, once a month,—because he hacks. But I have had this chopper nineteen years, and although I have cut up many thousand bullocks, its edge is as if fresh from the whetstone.
cards.author: Zhuangzi
cards.source: Chuang Tzu, chapter 3 (trans. Herbert A. Giles, 1889)
cards.more:
In this story, the cook of Prince Hui carves an ox so smoothly it looks like a dance. When the prince praises his skill, the cook explains that he no longer sees the whole animal. He follows its natural structure, sliding the blade through the gaps at the joints, so it never grinds against bone.

The prince says the cook has taught him how to take care of his life. Zhuangzi’s lesson: don’t force your way through things. Study how they are put together and work with that grain. It’s also a picture of mastery, effort refined until it looks effortless. Where are you hacking when you could be cutting?

cards.text: Arise! Awake! Having reached the Great Ones (illumined Teachers), gain understanding. The path is as sharp as a razor, impassable and difficult to travel, so the wise declare.
cards.author: Katha Upanishad
cards.source: Katha Upanishad, Part 3, verse 14 (trans. Swami Paramananda, 1919)
cards.more:
The Katha Upanishad tells of Nachiketas, a boy who goes to the house of Death and refuses to leave without learning what happens after we die. Death, impressed by his persistence, teaches him about the deepest self, which he says is never born and never dies.

This verse is the wake-up call at the heart of that teaching. Understanding doesn’t arrive by accident: you seek out people who know more, and you accept that the path is narrow and demanding. Somerset Maugham took the title of his novel The Razor’s Edge from it. Is there a question you care about enough to be as stubborn as Nachiketas?

cards.title: Doing by not forcing
cards.text: Wu wei is often translated as ‘non-action’, but it doesn’t mean doing nothing. It means acting without strain or force, the way water finds its path or an expert moves without overthinking. Laozi says the Tao never forces anything, and yet nothing is left undone.
cards.author: Laozi
cards.source: Tao Te Ching, chapters 37 and 48
cards.more:
Wu wei is one of the core ideas of Taoism. The Tao Te Ching contrasts the sage, who acts in harmony with how things naturally unfold, with rulers and people who meddle, push and grasp, and so make things worse.

In modern terms it’s close to what psychologists call flow: full engagement without the feeling of strain. It applies to people too. Over-managing a team, a child or a relationship often backfires, while setting good conditions and stepping back works better. Next time you’re pushing hard and getting nowhere, ask where the grain runs, and whether you could go with it.

cards.title: The child at the well
cards.text: Mencius asked us to imagine suddenly seeing a small child about to fall into a well. Anyone, he said, would feel alarm and compassion: not to win the parents’ favour or the neighbours’ praise, but instantly. That flash shows the sprouts of goodness are in everyone.
cards.author: Mencius
cards.source: Mencius, Book 2A.6
cards.more:
Mencius, a Confucian thinker of the 4th century BC, argued that human nature is good. Not finished and perfect, but containing four ‘sprouts’: compassion, shame, respect and a sense of right and wrong. Like seedlings, they need cultivating, and they can be stunted by neglect or harsh conditions.

The later Confucian Xunzi argued the opposite: that people are innately bad and goodness has to be built through education and ritual. The debate still echoes today. Mencius’ practical advice is a gardener’s: notice your small moral impulses, like the urge to help or to apologise, and act on them before they wither.

cards.title: Keep a beginner’s mind
cards.text: Shunryu Suzuki warned that expertise can quietly narrow the mind: the surer we are, the fewer possibilities we notice. Zen practice, as he taught it, means keeping a beginner’s openness, and meeting even familiar things as if for the first time.
cards.author: Shunryu Suzuki
cards.source: Zen Mind, Beginner’s Mind (1970)
cards.more:
Suzuki was a Japanese Soto Zen priest who moved to the United States and founded the San Francisco Zen Center, one of the most influential Zen communities in the West. His book, edited from informal talks, became one of the most popular introductions to Zen.

Beginner’s mind, shoshin in Japanese, isn’t about pretending to know nothing. It’s about not letting what you know block what you could notice. Experts often miss things precisely because they already know what to expect. Try it with something routine, like your commute, a colleague or a meal. Look at it as if you had never seen it before.

cards.title: Laozi may never have existed
cards.text: The Tao Te Ching is traditionally credited to Laozi, said to be an older contemporary of Confucius. But modern scholars are divided: some see him as largely or wholly legendary, and the text itself seems to have been transmitted and added to over time.
cards.author: Laozi
cards.source: Wikipedia: Laozi
cards.more:
Laozi simply means ‘Old Master’. The best-known legend has him growing weary of a declining kingdom and heading west to live as a hermit. At the frontier gate, a guard named Yinxi recognised him and asked him to write down his wisdom before leaving. The result, supposedly, was the Tao Te Ching.

Archaeology has added twists. Bamboo slips found at Guodian in 1993, dated to before 300 BC, contain early versions of parts of the text, which supports the idea of a book that grew over time. That suits Taoism: a text about the nameless Way, by an author who barely has a name himself.

cards.title: A tiny book, endlessly translated
cards.text: The Tao Te Ching runs to only about 5,200 to 5,500 Chinese characters in 81 short chapters. Yet it is one of the most translated texts in world literature, often ranked next to the Bible.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Tao Te Ching
cards.more:
The book was first translated into a European language, French, in the early 19th century, and since then translators have kept coming back to it. Part of the reason is its style: short, paradoxical lines with few grammatical markers, which leave a lot of room for interpretation. Compare any two English versions of the same chapter and they can read like different poems.

That’s worth remembering whenever you see a neat ‘Lao Tzu quote’ online. Many are loose modern paraphrases, and some aren’t in the book at all. Older public-domain translations, like James Legge’s, are clunkier but closer to the text, and free to read.

cards.title: Zen literally means meditation
cards.text: ‘Zen’ is the Japanese reading of the Chinese ‘Chan’, which comes from the Sanskrit dhyāna, meaning meditation. The school took shape in Tang dynasty China by blending Indian Mahayana Buddhism with Taoist ideas, then spread to Korea, Vietnam and Japan.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Zen
cards.more:
The name is the whole programme. Zen puts meditation, rather than studying scriptures or performing rituals, at the centre of practice. In Korea the same tradition is called Seon, and in Vietnam Thiền.

The Taoist influence shows in Zen’s love of paradox, simplicity and nature, and in its suspicion of explanations that get in the way of direct experience. That mix later shaped Japanese gardens, tea ceremony and ink painting. So when something is called ‘very zen’ today, it’s borrowing from a 1,000-plus-year-old fusion of Indian and Chinese thought, whose core instruction is simply to sit and pay attention.

cards.title: Are you the dreamer or the dream?
cards.text: Zhuangzi dreamed he was a butterfly, fluttering about, unaware he was Zhuangzi. Then he woke up. Was he a man who had dreamed of being a butterfly, or a butterfly now dreaming it was a man? How would you tell?
cards.author: Zhuangzi
cards.source: Chuang Tzu, chapter 2 (trans. Herbert A. Giles, 1889)
cards.more:
This is one of the most famous passages in Chinese philosophy. Western thinkers raised a similar doubt much later; Descartes worried he could never be completely sure he wasn’t dreaming. But Zhuangzi’s mood is different. He isn’t anxious about certainty. He enjoys the puzzle, and ends by noting that there must be some difference between a man and a butterfly, and calling the shift between them a transformation.

His deeper point is that the lines we draw between self and world, waking and dreaming, are less fixed than they feel. Instead of clinging to one identity, he suggests flowing with change. Hold your certainties a little more lightly.

cards.title: The sound of one hand
cards.text: You know the sound of two hands clapping. What is the sound of one hand? Don’t reach for a clever answer. Stay with the question, and notice what your mind does when logic runs out.
cards.author: Hakuin Ekaku
cards.source: Koan devised by Hakuin Ekaku, 18th-century Japan
cards.more:
This koan comes from the Japanese Zen master Hakuin Ekaku, who in later life used it to stir up ‘great doubt’ in beginners. Koans are puzzles used in Zen training, especially in the Rinzai school, and they are designed so that ordinary reasoning can’t crack them.

The aim isn’t to find the right answer but to wear out the habit of treating everything as a problem for the thinking mind. Students may work on one koan for months or years, presenting responses to a teacher. You don’t need a monastery to try the spirit of it: sit with a question you can’t solve, without rushing to resolve it.

cards.title: The oldest dated printed book
cards.text: The oldest printed book that carries a date is a Chinese copy of the Diamond Sutra from 868. A note at the end says a man named Wang Jie had it made for universal free distribution, on behalf of his two parents. Every page was carved, in reverse, into a single block of wood.
cards.source: Diamond Sutra, British Library copy (Or.8210/P.2), dated 11 May 868
cards.more:
The scroll was sealed for centuries in a cave library near Dunhuang, on the old Silk Road, and was bought by the explorer Aurel Stein in 1907. It is now in the British Library.

Woodblock printing was already old by then, which is why the scroll looks so polished: the frontispiece shows the Buddha teaching, cut with real skill. The catch was that every page needed its own carved block, so printing a new book meant carving everything from scratch.

That limitation is where this thread begins. The next big leap was to stop carving pages and start carving single characters that could be rearranged.

thread.title: How printing changed the world (8 cards)

cards.title: Movable type began with baked clay
cards.text: Around 1040, four centuries before Gutenberg, a Chinese commoner named Bi Sheng made movable type out of fired clay, one piece per character. He tried wood too, but it warped when it soaked up ink. We only know about him because a scholar, Shen Kuo, wrote his method down.
cards.source: Shen Kuo, Dream Pool Essays (c. 1088); Wikipedia, Bi Sheng
cards.more:
Bi Sheng's type pieces were set in an iron frame on a bed of wax and resin, warmed so the type stuck, then pressed flat and printed. Afterwards the frame was warmed again and the characters were sorted back into cases for reuse.

Shen Kuo noted that the method only paid off for large print runs, and that is the key to why it didn't take over in China. Chinese writing needs thousands of distinct characters, so setting type was slow, and woodblocks stayed competitive for centuries.

The idea was right. It just needed a writing system with fewer symbols, or a sturdier material, to really shine.

thread.title: How printing changed the world (8 cards)

cards.title: Korea printed with metal first
cards.text: The oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type is not the Gutenberg Bible. It is the Jikji, a collection of Buddhist teachings printed at Heungdeok Temple in Korea in 1377, 78 years earlier. Only its second volume survives, and it lives in the national library in Paris.
cards.source: UNESCO Memory of the World register (2001); Wikipedia, Jikji
cards.more:
Metal type solved the durability problem that dogged clay and wood. Korean printers cast characters in bronze, and the royal court backed large printing projects in the following century.

The surviving volume left Korea in the late 1800s, when a French diplomat collected it in Seoul. It ended up in the Bibliotheque nationale de France, and Korea has asked for it back for decades. UNESCO added it to its Memory of the World register in 2001.

So metal type existed in East Asia before Europe. What Europe was about to add was a whole system for doing it fast and cheap.

thread.title: How printing changed the world (8 cards)

cards.title: Gutenberg's real invention was a system
cards.text: Johannes Gutenberg finished his Bible in Mainz around 1455. Somewhere between 160 and 185 copies were printed, about three quarters on paper and the rest on calfskin vellum. Forty-nine survive in at least substantial part, and they are among the most valuable books on Earth.
cards.source: Wikipedia, Gutenberg Bible
cards.more:
Gutenberg didn't invent printing, or even movable type. What he pulled together was a working system: a hand mould for casting thousands of identical metal letters quickly, a metal alloy that melted easily and set hard, an oil-based ink that clung to metal, and a screw press adapted from wine and paper making.

The Latin alphabet helped him enormously. A few dozen letters, plus punctuation and variants, is a lot easier to cast and set than thousands of Chinese characters.

Gutenberg himself went broke and lost control of his shop to his financial backer. His method, though, was about to escape Mainz.

thread.title: How printing changed the world (8 cards)

cards.title: Twenty million books in fifty years
cards.text: In 1450 Gutenberg's shop in Mainz was the only print shop in Europe. By 1500, around 270 European cities had presses, and they had turned out more than 20 million copies. By 1600 the running total was somewhere between 150 and 200 million.
cards.source: Wikipedia, Printing press (citing Buringh and van Zanden, 2009, and the British Library's Incunabula Short Title Catalogue)
cards.more:
Printers were traveling craftsmen, and many of them were trained in Mainz. They moved to wherever there was paper, money and readers, and Venice became the giant: by some counts a third of Italy's printers worked there.

Books printed before 1501 have their own name, incunabula, from the Latin for cradle or swaddling clothes, because this was print in its infancy.

The price of a book fell sharply, and for the first time a scholar could own the same edition as a colleague hundreds of miles away and point to the same page. That shared, fixed text mattered almost as much as the numbers. The next card shows what happened when one angry monk got hold of it.

thread.title: How printing changed the world (8 cards)

cards.title: Luther, the first bestselling author
cards.text: By around 1520 Martin Luther was the most published author in Europe. Printers across Germany ran 291 editions of his 45 original works, and between 1518 and 1520 they put about 300,000 copies into circulation. Both the pope and secular rulers were caught off guard by how fast his ideas spread.
cards.source: Wikipedia, Printing press (citing Pettegree, Brand Luther, 2015)
cards.more:
Luther's 95 Theses of 1517 were written in Latin for academic debate. What made him famous was what came next: short, punchy pamphlets in German, cheap enough for ordinary townspeople, and printed in the thousands by printers who knew a bestseller when they saw one.

Earlier reformers like Jan Hus had been silenced. Luther couldn't be, because by the time authorities tried to suppress a pamphlet it had already been reprinted in a dozen cities.

The historian Andrew Pettegree argues the Reformation also created a market for printed news, as printers kept their new readers hooked with topical pamphlets.

thread.title: How printing changed the world (8 cards)

cards.title: Printing made knowledge pile up
cards.text: Elizabeth Eisenstein argued that the press didn't just make more books. It made identical ones. Once thousands of readers had the exact same maps, tables and diagrams, errors could be spotted, reported and fixed in the next edition, so knowledge started to accumulate instead of slowly decaying with every hand copy.
cards.author: Elizabeth Eisenstein
cards.source: The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (1979)
cards.more:
Before print, every copy of a text was a little different, and every copying introduced new mistakes. Scholars spent their energy trying to recover what the original said.

Eisenstein's big book, two volumes and some 750 pages, argued that standardization and preservation were the press's quiet superpowers. Astronomers could compare the same star tables. Anatomists could correct each other's drawings. She saw this as an essential ingredient of both the Reformation and the Scientific Revolution.

Historians still argue about how far to push her thesis, but it reframed the question. The press wasn't only a faster pen. It changed how knowledge itself behaved.

thread.title: How printing changed the world (8 cards)

cards.text: ...printing, gunpowder, and the compass. For these three have changed the appearance and state of the whole world: first in literature, then in warfare, and lastly in navigation...
cards.author: Francis Bacon
cards.source: Novum Organum, Book 1, Aphorism 129 (1620), ed. Joseph Devey
cards.more:
Bacon wrote this barely 170 years after Gutenberg, and he already saw printing as one of three inventions that had remade the world, all of them, as he noted, unknown to the ancients. He didn't know that all three had roots in China.

That's a nice way to close this thread. A technology born in Tang dynasty woodblocks, refined with clay and then metal type in China and Korea, and turned into a mass system in Mainz, ended up powering the Reformation, the Scientific Revolution, and Bacon's own project of building knowledge through shared, checkable evidence.

Every feed you scroll, this one included, is a distant descendant.

thread.title: How printing changed the world (8 cards)

cards.title: Cleopatra and the Moon landing
cards.text: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid. The pyramid went up around 2600 BC. Cleopatra died in 30 BC, roughly 2,570 years later. Apollo 11 landed in 1969, about 2,000 years after her.
cards.source: Wikipedia, Great Pyramid of Giza; Cleopatra
cards.more:
We tend to file everything Egyptian under one heading, ancient, but the civilization ran for about three thousand years. To Cleopatra, the Great Pyramid was already a monument from deep antiquity, about as old to her as the Bronze Age is to us.

She also wasn't ethnically Egyptian. She belonged to the Ptolemies, a Macedonian Greek dynasty founded by one of Alexander the Great's generals, and she is said to have been the first of her line to learn the Egyptian language.

It's a useful habit: whenever two things feel like they belong to the same era, check the dates. The gaps are often wider than the gap between them and us.

cards.title: Oxford is older than the Aztecs
cards.text: Teaching at Oxford was going on by 1096. The Aztec capital, Tenochtitlan, wasn't founded until 1325, and the Aztec Empire itself formed in 1428. So by the time the Aztecs built their empire, Oxford had been teaching students for more than 300 years.
cards.source: Wikipedia, University of Oxford; Tenochtitlan
cards.more:
This one scrambles our mental timeline because we file the Aztecs under ancient and Oxford under modern. In fact the Aztec Empire was young and short-lived: it lasted less than a century before the Spanish conquest destroyed Tenochtitlan in 1521.

At its height Tenochtitlan, built on an island in Lake Texcoco, was one of the largest cities in the world, with causeways, canals and an aqueduct. Mexico City now stands on its ruins.

Oxford has no exact founding date. It grew gradually, and got a boost in 1167 when Henry II banned English students from studying at the University of Paris.

cards.title: Napoleon wasn't actually short
cards.text: Napoleon was recorded as 5 feet 2 inches, but in old French units. That works out to about 1.67 metres, just under 5 feet 6 inches in English measure, close to average for a Frenchman of his day. The legend of the tiny tyrant was built from a unit mix-up and British propaganda.
cards.source: Wikipedia, Napoleon complex
cards.more:
The French inch, the pouce, was longer than the English inch, so the same number meant a taller man. English readers saw 5 foot 2 and pictured someone much smaller.

British cartoonists, especially James Gillray, happily drew him as a tantrum-throwing little man, and the image stuck. His nickname, le petit caporal, the little corporal, was actually a term of affection from his soldiers, not a comment on his height. He was also often surrounded by his Imperial Guard, who had minimum height requirements.

The Napoleon complex, the idea that short men overcompensate with aggression, is named after a man who wasn't short.

cards.title: Vikings didn't wear horned helmets
cards.text: There's no evidence that Viking warriors wore horned helmets. The image is a 19th-century invention, popularized by productions of Richard Wagner's Norse operas, which put horns and wings on their heroes. Real Viking helmets, the few that survive, were plain rounded iron caps.
cards.source: Wikipedia, Horned helmet
cards.more:
Horns would be a liability in a fight: something for an opponent's blade to catch, and awkward in a shield wall. The best-preserved Viking-age helmet, found at Gjermundbu in Norway in 1943, is a simple iron cap with a spectacle-like guard around the eyes.

Horned helmets did exist in Scandinavia, but much earlier, in the Bronze Age, and they seem to have been ceremonial.

The costumes for the first Bayreuth staging of Wagner's Ring cycle in 1876 helped fix the look in the public imagination, along with Romantic-era painters who loved a dramatic silhouette. From there it went to cartoons, sports mascots and Halloween costumes.

cards.title: Medieval people knew the Earth was round
cards.text: Educated Europeans in the Middle Ages did not think the Earth was flat. Its roundness had been accepted since the ancient Greeks. The idea that Columbus had to convince people otherwise was popularized much later, notably by Washington Irving's romanticized 1828 biography of Columbus.
cards.source: Wikipedia, Myth of the flat Earth
cards.more:
The argument about Columbus was real, but it was about size, not shape. His critics thought the Earth was too big for a ship to reach Asia by sailing west, and they were right. Columbus had badly underestimated the distance. He only survived because an unknown continent was in the way.

Medieval scholars learned about a spherical Earth from Greek sources and wrote about it openly. A popular medieval textbook was literally called On the Sphere.

The flat-Earth myth spread in the 1800s partly because it suited a story some writers wanted to tell, of science bravely battling religious ignorance. Historians now see that story as heavily exaggerated.

cards.text: ...right, as the world goes, is only in question between equals in power, while the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.
cards.author: Thucydides
cards.source: History of the Peloponnesian War, Book 5, the Melian Dialogue (c. 400 BC), trans. Richard Crawley
cards.more:
In 416 BC Athens sent a fleet to the small island of Melos, which wanted to stay neutral in the war with Sparta. Thucydides reconstructs the negotiation as a dialogue, and these are the words he gives the Athenian envoys. They don't pretend to have justice on their side. They simply point out that they have the power.

The Melians appealed to fairness, the gods and hope of Spartan help. None came. Athens took the island, killed the men, and enslaved the women and children.

The dialogue is still read in courses on international relations as the founding text of political realism, and as a warning about what power does to those who hold it.

cards.text: His reign is marked by the rare advantage of furnishing very few materials for history; which is, indeed, little more than the register of the crimes, follies, and misfortunes of mankind.
cards.author: Edward Gibbon
cards.source: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, Vol. 1, ch. 3 (1776)
cards.more:
Gibbon is describing the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius, who ruled from 138 to 161 AD. His point is a sly one: a good reign leaves historians with almost nothing to write about, because history mostly records disasters.

The line is often quoted alone as a gloomy verdict on humanity, but in context it's almost a compliment. Peace, competence and quiet prosperity simply don't generate dramatic events.

It's worth remembering when reading any history, or any news. What gets recorded is what went wrong. The long stretches when things went fine, which is where most people actually lived, barely leave a trace.

cards.text: ...in peace the sons bury their fathers, but in war the fathers bury their sons.
cards.author: Herodotus
cards.source: The Histories, Book 1, ch. 87 (c. 430 BC), trans. G. C. Macaulay
cards.more:
Herodotus puts these words in the mouth of Croesus, the fabulously rich king of Lydia, after his empire has fallen to Cyrus the Great of Persia. Croesus had attacked Persia after consulting the oracle at Delphi, which told him that if he went to war, a great empire would be destroyed. It was. His own.

In Herodotus's telling, Cyrus asks who persuaded him to make war, and Croesus blames the god of the Greeks, then adds this reflection.

Herodotus is often called the father of history, and this is one of his most enduring lines: war reverses the natural order of grief.

cards.title: Did wheat domesticate us?
cards.text: Yuval Noah Harari argues the Agricultural Revolution was a bad deal for most individuals. Compared with foragers, early farmers worked longer hours, ate a narrower diet and faced famine and disease. What farming did deliver was more people. In his telling, wheat used us to spread across the planet as much as we used it.
cards.author: Yuval Noah Harari
cards.source: Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind, ch. 5 (English edition, 2014)
cards.more:
Harari's point is that we shouldn't confuse a species' success with individual wellbeing. Measured in sheer numbers of copies, wheat and humans both won big. Measured in hours of toil, back problems and tooth decay, many early farmers arguably lost.

Why didn't people go back? Because each small step seemed sensible at the time, and once populations grew to depend on harvests, there was no route back to foraging. He calls this a trap: luxuries become necessities and create new obligations.

Not every archaeologist agrees with his framing, but it's a sharp question to carry around. Which of today's conveniences are quietly doing the same thing?

cards.title: Why Eurasia's shape mattered
cards.text: Jared Diamond argues that geography, not the people in it, explains why some societies conquered others. Eurasia stretches east to west, so crops and animals could spread along similar climates. The Americas and Africa run north to south, across climate zones, which slowed the spread of farming.
cards.author: Jared Diamond
cards.source: Guns, Germs, and Steel (1997)
cards.more:
Diamond starts from a question a New Guinean politician named Yali put to him: why did Europeans end up with so much cargo, and New Guineans with so little?

His answer chains together advantages. Eurasia happened to have more wild plants and large animals that could be domesticated. Farming produced food surpluses, dense populations, specialists and states. Living close to livestock bred epidemic diseases, and with them, immunity. When Europeans reached the Americas, germs killed far more people than guns did.

Critics say the book downplays culture, choices and chance. But it changed how a generation thinks about inequality between nations.

cards.title: Governments that act against themselves
cards.text: Barbara Tuchman studied what she called folly: governments pursuing policies contrary to their own interest, even when warned at the time and offered a workable alternative. She traced it from the Trojans dragging in the wooden horse to Britain losing its American colonies and the United States in Vietnam.
cards.author: Barbara Tuchman
cards.source: The March of Folly: From Troy to Vietnam (1984)
cards.more:
Tuchman set a strict test. It doesn't count as folly just because it looks foolish in hindsight. People at the time had to see the danger and say so, and a better option had to be available. The policy also had to be a group effort that outlasted any one ruler.

Her cases include the Renaissance popes, whose corruption helped provoke the Protestant Reformation, and British ministers who kept taxing and provoking the American colonies despite loud warnings in Parliament.

The common thread is what she called wooden-headedness: sticking to a fixed idea while ignoring contrary evidence. It's a failure mode that applies to companies and people too.

cards.title: Mammoths or pyramids?
cards.text: Which came first: the last woolly mammoths, or the Great Pyramid of Giza?
cards.source: Wikipedia, Woolly mammoth
cards.more:
The pyramid. It was built around 2600 BC, and the last known woolly mammoths were still alive on Wrangel Island, in the Arctic Ocean off Siberia, until about 4,000 years ago, around 2000 BC.

Most mammoths had vanished from the mainland by about 10,000 years ago, as the climate warmed and human hunters spread. But small isolated populations hung on. One survived on St. Paul Island in Alaska until about 5,600 years ago, and the Wrangel group outlasted it by more than a thousand years.

So while Egyptians were cutting limestone blocks and writing in hieroglyphs, mammoths were still walking around on an island at the top of the world.

cards.title: Born the same day
cards.text: Two men who reshaped the 19th century were born on exactly the same day, 12 February 1809, one in a Kentucky log cabin and one in a comfortable English house. Can you name them?
cards.source: Wikipedia, Charles Darwin; Abraham Lincoln
cards.more:
Abraham Lincoln and Charles Darwin. Lincoln was born in a one-room cabin in Hardin County, Kentucky. Darwin was born in Shrewsbury, England, into a wealthy family of doctors and industrialists.

Their great works landed within a few years of each other. Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859. Lincoln was elected president in 1860 and issued the Emancipation Proclamation in 1863.

Both men also shared a hatred of slavery. Darwin had seen it firsthand in Brazil on the Beagle voyage and wrote about it with disgust. The coincidence of birthdays means nothing, of course, but it's a vivid reminder of how much one generation can change.

cards.title: The man who memorised nonsense
cards.text: In the 1880s, Hermann Ebbinghaus memorised lists of nonsense syllables like WID and ZOF, then tested himself after different delays. Forgetting, he found, is fast at first and then slows down: a large share of what you learn is gone within a day or two unless you do something about it.
cards.source: Hermann Ebbinghaus, Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology (1885)
cards.more:
Ebbinghaus used nonsense on purpose, so meaning and prior knowledge could not help him. He was his own only subject, which is a real limitation, yet a 2015 replication by Jaap Murre and Joeri Dros found a very similar curve.

Meaningful material is forgotten more slowly than nonsense, so do not treat his exact percentages as gospel. The shape is the lesson: a steep loss early, then a long, slow tail.

That shape sets up the rest of this thread. If forgetting is the default, the question is not how to cram more in, but how to make what goes in survive. The next cards cover the tools with the best evidence.

thread.title: How to learn so it sticks, in 7 cards

cards.title: Spread it out
cards.text: A 2006 review of decades of memory experiments found that spaced practice beat massed practice, or cramming, in 259 of 271 comparisons. Same total study time, very different results. Splitting study into sessions with gaps between them is one of the most reliable findings in learning research.
cards.source: Cepeda et al., Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks, Psychological Bulletin (2006)
cards.more:
Ebbinghaus himself noticed the spacing effect, and it has been replicated for well over a century, across ages, subjects and even other species.

Why it works is still debated. One popular idea is that letting a memory fade a little before you revisit it forces a more effortful recall, which strengthens it more than reviewing something you still remember perfectly.

The best gap depends on how long you need to remember. Later work by Cepeda and colleagues suggests gaps of very roughly 10 to 20 percent of the time until you need the knowledge, shrinking proportionally for longer horizons. Flashcard apps that schedule reviews for you do this arithmetic automatically.

thread.title: How to learn so it sticks, in 7 cards

cards.title: Testing beats rereading
cards.text: Students read a short passage, then either reread it or took practice tests on it. Five minutes later, the rereaders did slightly better. A week later, the testers remembered far more. Pulling information out of memory strengthens it more than putting it in again.
cards.source: Roediger & Karpicke, Test-Enhanced Learning, Psychological Science (2006)
cards.more:
This is the testing effect, also called retrieval practice. A test is not just a measurement; the act of recalling changes the memory, making it easier to find next time.

It works best combined with the spacing from the last card, and with feedback so mistakes do not stick. It even helps when you fail to recall, as long as you check the answer afterwards.

Practical versions: close the book and write down everything you remember from a chapter. Answer a flashcard out loud before flipping it. Explain an idea without notes. Ask a friend to quiz you. All of this feels harder than rereading, which is the subject of card five.

thread.title: How to learn so it sticks, in 7 cards

cards.title: Mix up your practice
cards.text: Nate Kornell and Robert Bjork had people learn painters' styles either one artist at a time or all mixed together. Mixing worked better for recognising new paintings, yet most participants believed the one-at-a-time approach had helped them more. Interleaving forces you to notice what makes each thing different.
cards.author: Nate Kornell and Robert Bjork
cards.source: Learning Concepts and Categories, Psychological Science (2008)
cards.more:
Blocked practice means doing all the problems of one type, then all of the next. Interleaving means shuffling them. Studies by Doug Rohrer and colleagues found the same pattern in maths: students who practised mixed problem sets did much better on later tests, because they had to work out which method each problem needed, rather than reusing the one from the chapter heading.

Interleaving feels slower and messier, and early performance looks worse. That is a big part of why people avoid it.

Try it: mix old and new topics in a revision session, alternate between scales and pieces when practising an instrument, or shuffle your flashcard decks instead of studying one category at a time.

thread.title: How to learn so it sticks, in 7 cards

cards.title: Why easy studying fools you
cards.text: Robert Bjork coined the term desirable difficulties: conditions that make learning feel harder but make it last. Rereading and highlighting feel smooth, and the smoothness gets mistaken for mastery. Spacing, testing and mixing feel clumsy, and that clumsiness is often the learning happening.
cards.author: Robert A. Bjork
cards.source: Memory and metamemory considerations in the training of human beings, in Metacognition (1994)
cards.more:
The trap is that we judge our learning by how fluent it feels in the moment. Rereading a chapter makes the text familiar, and familiarity feels like knowing. But recognising something on the page is very different from producing it on a blank sheet.

Not every difficulty is desirable. Bjork's point is that a difficulty helps when it makes you do the kind of mental work you will need later, like recalling, comparing and telling things apart. Confusing explanations or background noise are just hard.

A quick check: if a study session felt pleasantly easy, you probably overestimated what you learned. Test yourself before you decide you are done.

thread.title: How to learn so it sticks, in 7 cards

cards.text: I took some of the papers, and, making short hints of the sentiment in each sentence, laid them by a few days, and then, without looking at the book, try'd to compleat the papers again... Then I compared my Spectator with the original, discovered some of my faults, and corrected them.
cards.author: Benjamin Franklin
cards.source: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, part one (written 1771)
cards.more:
As a teenager, Franklin taught himself to write by rebuilding essays from The Spectator. Look at what he built: spacing (he waited a few days), retrieval (he rewrote without looking), and feedback (he compared his version with the original and fixed his mistakes).

He varied it too. He turned some essays into verse and later back into prose to stretch his vocabulary, and jumbled his notes, then tried to restore their order, to learn how to structure an argument.

The same loop works for almost any skill. Produce something from memory, compare it with an expert's version, and work on the gaps. It is far less comfortable than admiring good work, which is exactly why it works.

thread.title: How to learn so it sticks, in 7 cards

cards.title: One routine that uses all of it
cards.text: Make It Stick boils decades of learning research down to a few habits. Quiz yourself instead of rereading. Space out your reviews. Mix related topics. Try to answer before you are taught. Reflect on what went wrong. None of it needs special tools, just a willingness to feel less fluent.
cards.author: Peter C. Brown, Henry Roediger and Mark McDaniel
cards.source: Make It Stick: The Science of Successful Learning (2014)
cards.more:
Here is the thread as one routine. After a lecture, chapter or meeting, close it and write down what you remember (testing). Check it against the source and note the gaps (Franklin's loop). Schedule a review a few days later, then another a week after that (spacing, against Ebbinghaus's curve). When you review, mix in older material (interleaving).

Expect it to feel harder and slower than rereading. That feeling is the desirable difficulty, not a sign of failure.

The authors also stress calibration: use tests to find out what you actually know, rather than trusting a sense of familiarity. Most people who try this discover they knew less than they thought, then remember more than they expected.

thread.title: How to learn so it sticks, in 7 cards

cards.text: Reading maketh a full man; conference a ready man; and writing an exact man.
cards.author: Francis Bacon
cards.source: Essays, 'Of Studies' (1625 edition)
cards.more:
In Bacon's English, conference means conversation and debate, and exact means precise. Each activity trains something different. Reading stocks your mind. Talking with others makes you quick at using what you know. Writing forces you to pin vague ideas down, because a sentence on paper cannot hide behind a feeling of understanding.

That last point is why writing is such a strong learning tool. Many people only discover they do not understand something when they try to explain it in writing and get stuck halfway.

A balanced week might include all three: read something substantial, argue about it with someone, and write a page on what you now think.

cards.text: As the art of reading (after a certain stage in one's education) is the art of skipping, so the art of being wise is the art of knowing what to overlook.
cards.author: William James
cards.source: The Principles of Psychology, vol. 2, ch. 22 'Reasoning' (1890)
cards.more:
James is describing how expert thinking works. As you get better at something, you stop processing every detail and start seeing only the features that matter. A strong chess player glances at a board and ignores most of it; a beginner has to consider every piece.

This cuts against the urge to read every word and keep every note. Skimming to find what matters, then reading that part slowly, is a skill, not a shortcut.

The hard part is choosing well what to overlook, and that depends on knowing what you are trying to do. Before you open a long report or book, write down the two or three questions you want it to answer.

cards.text: The second, to divide each of the difficulties under examination into as many parts as possible, and as might be necessary for its adequate solution.
cards.author: René Descartes
cards.source: Discourse on the Method, part II (1637; trans. John Veitch)
cards.more:
Descartes set himself four rules for thinking. Accept nothing as true that you do not clearly know. Break each difficulty into parts. Work from the simplest parts up to the complex ones. And review everything so completely that nothing is left out. This card is the second rule.

It is the one that travels best. A task like 'write the report' is paralysing; 'list the five sections' and 'draft the first paragraph of section one' are not. Programmers, mathematicians and anyone planning a project rely on the same move.

The phrase 'as might be necessary' matters. The aim is not to chop endlessly, but to keep splitting until each piece is something you can actually do or answer.

cards.text: People are generally better persuaded by the reasons which they have themselves discovered than by those which have come into the mind of others.
cards.author: Blaise Pascal
cards.source: Pensées, no. 10 (1670; trans. W. F. Trotter)
cards.more:
Pascal's observation explains why lectures and arguments so often fail. Telling someone the answer, however clearly, hands them a conclusion with no roots. Helping them find it gives them ownership and a path back to it.

Learning research points the same way. The generation effect, studied since the 1970s, shows that information you produce yourself, even from small cues, is remembered better than information you simply read.

This is useful for teaching, managing and parenting: ask the question that leads toward the insight rather than delivering it. In the pensée just before this one, Pascal adds a companion tip: to correct someone, first find the side from which they are right and admit it.

cards.title: A latticework of models
cards.text: Charlie Munger argued that isolated facts are nearly useless unless they hang on a latticework of models: big ideas from many fields, like compound interest, incentives, feedback loops and margin of safety. Someone with only one model, he warned, is the man with a hammer to whom every problem looks like a nail.
cards.author: Charlie Munger
cards.source: A Lesson on Elementary Worldly Wisdom, talk at USC Business School (1994)
cards.more:
Munger's point was that the world does not arrive sorted into academic departments. A business problem might be part psychology, part maths, part biology. If you know only one discipline, you will force everything into its frame.

He suggested learning the big ideas from each major field well enough to use them, not just to pass exams, and then checking a problem against several. He reckoned that around 80 or 90 important models do most of the work.

You can start small. Keep a list of models you understand, each with one real example. When facing a decision, run down the list and ask which ones apply.

cards.title: Invert, always invert
cards.text: Munger liked to repeat the mathematician Carl Jacobi's advice to invert problems. Instead of asking how to succeed, ask what would guarantee failure, then avoid it. In a 1986 graduation speech he described a good life by listing sure routes to a miserable one, like envy, resentment and unreliability.
cards.author: Charlie Munger
cards.source: Commencement speech at the Harvard School, Los Angeles (1986)
cards.more:
Inversion works because our minds are better at spotting what is clearly wrong than at designing what is ideal. Ask 'how could I make this team miserable?' and the answers come fast: unclear priorities, surprise deadlines, credit taken by others. Now you have a list to avoid.

Jacobi used the idea in mathematics, where attacking a problem from its converse or its negation often makes it easier. Proof by contradiction is the same move.

Try it on any plan: list the five fastest ways it could fail, and check you are not already doing any of them. It is a cousin of the premortem, and it takes two minutes.

cards.title: The cost of a quick check
cards.text: Cal Newport argues that the ability to focus without distraction on hard tasks is getting rarer just as it gets more valuable. He leans on Sophie Leroy's research on attention residue: after you switch tasks, part of your mind stays stuck on the last one, so even a quick check degrades the next stretch of work.
cards.author: Cal Newport
cards.source: Deep Work, part 1 (2016)
cards.more:
Leroy's 2009 experiments found that people who left one task unfinished and moved to another performed worse on the second, because their thoughts kept drifting back. A quick look at your inbox can leave residue long after you close it.

Newport's remedies are structural rather than motivational: schedule blocks of focused time in advance, batch shallow tasks like email together, and treat distraction-free work as a skill you practise, one that weakens without use.

You do not need a cabin in the woods. One protected 90-minute block a day, with your phone in another room, is enough to notice the difference.

cards.title: Don't judge a decision by its result
cards.text: Former poker champion Annie Duke warns against resulting: judging a decision by how it turned out. A drunk driver who gets home safely did not make a good choice. A sound bet can still lose. If you only learn from outcomes, you will learn the wrong lessons from luck.
cards.author: Annie Duke
cards.source: Thinking in Bets, ch. 1 (2018)
cards.more:
Duke opens her book with a famous American football call: a pass at the end of the 2015 Super Bowl that was intercepted and instantly branded one of the worst decisions ever. Her point is that the same call would have been praised if it had worked, and that a close look at the odds suggests it was defensible.

The fix is to separate the quality of a decision from the quality of its outcome. Ask what you knew at the time, what the options were, how you weighed the odds, and what you could have found out cheaply.

Thinking in probabilities helps. 'I'm 70% sure' leaves room for the 30%, so a bad result teaches you something instead of just stinging.

cards.title: Growth mindset, honestly
cards.text: Carol Dweck's research suggests that people who see ability as something that can grow handle setbacks better than people who see it as fixed. The idea has something to it, but large recent studies find its effects on school results are real yet modest, not life-changing.
cards.author: Carol Dweck
cards.source: Mindset: The New Psychology of Success (2006)
cards.more:
Dweck contrasts a fixed mindset, where failure reveals your limits, with a growth mindset, where failure is information about what to practise next. Praising effort and strategy rather than talent was one of her best-known recommendations.

The evidence has become more nuanced. A 2018 meta-analysis found weak overall links between mindset and achievement. A large 2019 national study in the US found that a short online mindset lesson raised grades slightly, mostly for lower-achieving students.

The useful version is not a poster slogan. It is concrete: when something goes wrong, ask what you would do differently next time, and then actually try it.

cards.title: Everyone's thesis took longer
cards.text: In a 1994 study, psychology students estimated their senior theses would take about 34 days. Even their worst-case guesses averaged under 49 days. The real average was 55.5 days, and only about 30% finished within the time they had predicted.
cards.source: Buehler, Griffin & Ross, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (1994)
cards.more:
Kahneman and Tversky named this the planning fallacy in 1979. We plan by imagining the specific steps going roughly as intended, and we underweight the dull fact that things rarely go as intended: illness, other people, revisions, plain procrastination.

The best-known fix is reference class forecasting. Instead of building an estimate from the inside, start from the outside: how long did similar projects actually take, for you or for others? Then adjust a little for what is genuinely different.

If you have no data, start collecting it. Write down estimates and actual times for a month. Most people find a fairly consistent multiplier, and using it is humbling and very useful.

cards.title: Chesterton's fence
cards.text: G. K. Chesterton imagined a reformer who finds a fence across a road and wants it gone because he sees no use for it. A wiser reformer says: first go and find out why it was put there. Only once you know its purpose can you judge whether removing it is safe.
cards.author: G. K. Chesterton
cards.source: The Thing, 'The Drift from Domesticity' (1929)
cards.more:
The principle is about second-order thinking. Rules, processes and habits often exist because of a problem nobody remembers anymore, precisely because the fence solved it. Remove it and the problem can return.

That does not mean every fence is wise. The burden is on you to understand before you remove, not to keep everything forever. Often you will find the reason is long gone and the fence can go.

In practice: before deleting that odd line of code, cancelling a meeting or cutting a step in a process, spend ten minutes asking who added it and why. The answer is usually cheaper than rediscovering it the hard way.

cards.title: Can you really multitask?
cards.text: Plenty of people say they are good at doing several things at once. What is actually happening in your head when you think you are multitasking?
cards.source: Monsell, Task switching, Trends in Cognitive Sciences (2003)
cards.more:
For anything that needs attention, you are mostly switching, not doing two things at once. Each switch has a cost: in lab tasks, people are slower and make more errors right after changing tasks than after repeating the same one, and the cost remains even when they are warned a switch is coming.

Each individual cost is small, often a fraction of a second, but it adds up over a day of constant toggling, and grows with more complex tasks. Add attention residue and the hidden price of just checking becomes clear.

The exception is pairing an automatic activity with a thinking one, like walking while talking. Two demanding tasks will always trade off against each other.

cards.title: Are you a visual learner?
cards.text: Most teachers and students believe people learn best when taught in their preferred style: visual, auditory or hands-on. Does matching teaching to a person's learning style actually improve learning?
cards.source: Pashler, McDaniel, Rohrer & Bjork, Psychological Science in the Public Interest (2008)
cards.more:
There is no good evidence that it does. In 2008, a panel led by Harold Pashler reviewed the research and set out what a proper test needs: sort learners by style, teach each group in more than one style, and check whether each group does best in its own style. Very few studies did this, and those that did mostly found no such match.

People do have preferences, and some subjects suit some formats: maps are visual, music is auditory. But the best format depends on the content, not the person.

The practical upshot is to stop limiting yourself. Combining words and pictures, and actively testing yourself, helps nearly everyone.

cards.title: Is 10,000 hours the magic number?
cards.text: Malcolm Gladwell's Outliers popularised the idea that about 10,000 hours of practice makes an expert. Is practice really what separates the best from everyone else?
cards.source: Macnamara, Hambrick & Oswald, Psychological Science (2014)
cards.more:
Practice matters a lot, but it is not the whole story, and 10,000 is not a rule. Anders Ericsson, whose violin research inspired the idea, objected that Gladwell oversimplified it: the figure was an average at one age, and the kind of practice mattered as much as the amount.

A 2014 meta-analysis by Brooke Macnamara and colleagues found deliberate practice explained about 26% of the differences in performance for games, 21% for music, 18% for sports, 4% for education and under 1% for professions. Starting age, aptitude, coaching and luck all play a part.

So practise, and practise well, with feedback and focus. Just do not expect a fixed number of hours to add up to mastery.

cards.title: Probability was born over a dice game
cards.text: Around 1654, a gambler asked Blaise Pascal how to split the pot fairly when a game is stopped before it ends. Pascal worked it out in letters with Pierre de Fermat. Their answer, counting the ways each player could still win, laid the foundations of the mathematics of probability.
cards.source: Pascal-Fermat correspondence on the problem of points (1654)
cards.more:
The puzzle is called the problem of points. Suppose two players are racing to win a set number of rounds, and the game stops when one needs 1 more win and the other needs 3. Splitting the pot by rounds already won seems fair, but it is not. Pascal and Fermat's insight was to look forward: list every way the remaining rounds could go, and divide the pot by each player's share of those futures.

Here the second player needs three wins in a row, a chance of 1 in 8, so a fair split is 7 to 1.

That shift, from what has happened to the weighted set of what could happen, is the core of expected value. The rest of this thread builds on it.

thread.title: Probability will fool you, in 7 cards

cards.title: The birthday puzzle
cards.text: How many people need to be in a room for there to be a better than even chance that two of them share a birthday? Make a guess before you open the answer.
cards.source: The birthday problem (assuming 365 equally likely birthdays)
cards.more:
Just 23. With 23 people, the chance of a shared birthday is about 50.7%. With 70 people it is over 99.9%.

Most guesses are far higher because we picture someone matching our own birthday. But the question is about any pair, and 23 people form 253 different pairs. Each pair has only a small chance of matching, but there are a lot of pairs.

The neat way to calculate it is to find the chance that nobody matches: 365/365 × 364/365 × 363/365 and so on for 23 people, which comes to about 49.3%. Computing the opposite event is one of the most useful tricks in probability, and it explains why coincidences are far more common than they feel.

thread.title: Probability will fool you, in 7 cards

cards.title: The Monty Hall problem
cards.text: You pick one of three doors. A car is behind one, goats behind the other two. The host, who knows where the car is, opens one of the other doors to reveal a goat, then offers to let you switch. Should you?
cards.source: Marilyn vos Savant, 'Ask Marilyn', Parade (1990)
cards.more:
Yes. Switching wins two times out of three; sticking wins one time in three.

Your first pick is right one time in three, and nothing the host does changes that. So two times in three the car is behind one of the other doors, and the host has just shown you which of them it is not. Switching collects that two-thirds. If it still feels wrong, imagine 100 doors. You pick one, the host opens 98 goats and leaves one other door closed. Would you switch now?

When Marilyn vos Savant gave this answer in 1990, about 10,000 readers wrote in, nearly 1,000 of them with PhDs, mostly to say she was wrong. Even Paul Erdős stayed unconvinced until he saw a computer simulation.

thread.title: Probability will fool you, in 7 cards

cards.title: How evidence should change your mind
cards.text: Thomas Bayes, an English minister, worked out how evidence should change a belief. Start with how plausible something was beforehand. Then ask how much more likely the new evidence is if it is true than if it is false. Combine the two. The result, published after his death in 1763, is Bayes' theorem.
cards.author: Thomas Bayes
cards.source: An Essay towards solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances, Philosophical Transactions (1763)
cards.more:
In odds form it is pleasingly simple: new odds = old odds × how much more likely the evidence is if the idea is true. If something was a long shot at odds of 1 to 9, and you see evidence three times as likely if it is true, the odds become 3 to 9, which is 1 to 3, a 25% chance.

Two lessons fall out. The starting point matters: a single piece of evidence cannot make a rare thing likely on its own. And beliefs should move step by step with each piece of evidence, not jump between certain and impossible.

Bayes's friend Richard Price edited and published the essay. The next card shows what goes wrong when we ignore the starting point.

thread.title: Probability will fool you, in 7 cards

cards.title: You tested positive. How worried?
cards.text: A disease affects 1 in 100 people. A test catches 90% of real cases, and wrongly flags 9% of healthy people. You test positive. Roughly what is the chance you actually have the disease?
cards.source: Gigerenzer & Hoffrage, How to improve Bayesian reasoning without instruction, Psychological Review (1995)
cards.more:
About 9%, not 90%. Picture 1,000 people. Ten have the disease, and 9 of them test positive. Of the 990 healthy people, about 89 test positive by mistake. That makes 98 positives, of which only 9 are real: roughly 1 in 11.

This is the base rate fallacy. The rarity of the disease, its base rate, outweighs the accuracy of the test. Gerd Gigerenzer and others found that many doctors get questions like this badly wrong when given percentages, and far more often right when given the same information as counts of people, as above.

So when percentages confuse you, translate them into a crowd of 1,000 and count. And a positive result usually means: get a second test.

thread.title: Probability will fool you, in 7 cards

cards.title: Black came up 26 times
cards.text: In 1913, the roulette wheel at the Monte Carlo Casino landed on black 26 times in a row. Gamblers lost millions of francs betting on red, sure it was overdue. But a wheel has no memory: on every one of those spins, red was exactly as likely as before.
cards.source: Monte Carlo Casino (1913), the standard example of the gambler's fallacy
cards.more:
This is the gambler's fallacy: believing a random process will balance itself out in the short run. The law of large numbers does say that over many spins the share of black settles near its expected value, but it gets there by swamping early streaks with more data, not by correcting them.

A run of 26 of either colour on a wheel with one zero has a probability of about 1 in 68 million. Rare, but with enough wheels spinning for enough years, rare things happen somewhere.

The same error shows up when people feel a girl is due after three boys, or that a falling stock must bounce. Before expecting things to even out, ask whether the process has any memory.

thread.title: Probability will fool you, in 7 cards

cards.title: Out of how many?
cards.text: Psychologist Gerd Gigerenzer argues most people are not hopeless at probability, just badly served by how it is presented. Turn percentages into counts, ask for the base rate, and think about all the ways things could turn out, not just the one story in front of you.
cards.author: Gerd Gigerenzer
cards.source: Calculated Risks: How to Know When Numbers Deceive You (2002)
cards.more:
This thread as a checklist. Look forward at all the possible outcomes, as Pascal and Fermat did. Expect coincidences, because many small chances add up, as in the birthday puzzle. Ask what the person giving you information knows, as with Monty Hall. Start from the base rate and update with evidence, like Bayes. Translate percentages into a crowd of people. And remember that dice and roulette wheels have no memory.

Gigerenzer calls this risk literacy and argues it can be taught, even to children, once numbers are presented as natural frequencies.

None of it needs heavy maths. It needs one habit: whenever you hear a probability, ask, out of how many?

thread.title: Probability will fool you, in 7 cards

cards.text: Mathematics, rightly viewed, possesses not only truth, but supreme beauty—a beauty cold and austere, like that of sculpture, without appeal to any part of our weaker nature...
cards.author: Bertrand Russell
cards.source: Mysticism and Logic, 'The Study of Mathematics' (1918; essay first published 1907)
cards.more:
Russell wrote this while deep in the work that became Principia Mathematica, an attempt to build mathematics from pure logic. For him the beauty lay in the certainty and economy of a proof: a few assumptions, a chain of steps, and a conclusion that could not be otherwise.

Many mathematicians describe the same feeling about results like Euclid's proof that the primes never run out, or Euler's identity, which ties e, i, π, 1 and 0 together in one short line.

If maths at school felt like a list of procedures, this is the part that usually got left out. The procedures are the scaffolding. The ideas they hold up are the sculpture.

cards.text: Thus mathematics may be defined as the subject in which we never know what we are talking about, nor whether what we are saying is true.
cards.author: Bertrand Russell
cards.source: Mysticism and Logic, 'Mathematics and the Metaphysicians' (1918; essay first published 1901)
cards.more:
It is a joke with a serious point. Russell is describing pure mathematics as logic: you start from assumptions and deduce what follows, without caring whether the assumptions describe anything real. A proof says 'if these, then that'. Whether 'these' are true is someone else's problem.

That is why mathematics is so reusable. The same theorems about abstract symmetry groups apply to crystals, Rubik's cubes and particle physics, because the maths never committed to what the objects were.

It also explains a common frustration. Asking 'but what is a vector, really?' misses that mathematicians mostly care about what vectors do: the rules they obey.

cards.text: At the moment when I put my foot on the step the idea came to me, without anything in my former thoughts seeming to have paved the way for it, that the transformations I had used to define the Fuchsian functions were identical with those of non-Euclidean geometry.
cards.author: Henri Poincaré
cards.source: Science and Method, book I, ch. 3 'Mathematical Creation' (1908; trans. G. B. Halsted, 1913)
cards.more:
Poincaré had worked hard on the problem for weeks, then left it behind for a geology trip. The answer arrived as he stepped onto a bus, in the middle of a conversation about something else. He checked it later at his leisure, and it was right.

He described a pattern in this and similar experiences: intense conscious work, then a break, then a sudden insight, then careful verification. He was clear that the sudden part never came without the hard part first.

Psychologists call the break incubation, and studies suggest it does help with some creative problems. The practical version: work hard on a problem, then walk away from it, and keep a notebook handy.

cards.text: The scientist does not study nature because it is useful; he studies it because he delights in it, and he delights in it because it is beautiful.
cards.author: Henri Poincaré
cards.source: Science and Method, book I, ch. 1 'The Choice of Facts' (1908; trans. G. B. Halsted, 1913)
cards.more:
Poincaré goes on to say he does not mean the beauty of colours and appearances, but a deeper beauty that comes from the harmonious order of the parts, something a pure intelligence can grasp. He argues this taste for simplicity and harmony is not a luxury; it steers scientists toward the facts and theories that turn out to matter.

Mathematicians still talk this way. An elegant proof is valued not only for being pretty, but because it usually shows why something is true, not just that it is.

If you are learning maths, watch for the moment a result stops feeling like a rule to memorise and starts feeling inevitable. That is the delight he meant.

cards.title: The primes never run out
cards.text: Suppose you had a complete list of primes. Multiply them all together and add 1. The result leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by any prime on your list, so it is either prime itself or built from primes you missed. Either way, the list was incomplete. This argument is about 2,300 years old.
cards.author: Euclid
cards.source: Elements, book IX, proposition 20 (c. 300 BC)
cards.more:
This is one of the most admired proofs in mathematics: it is short, needs no equipment, and settles a question about infinity with a finite argument.

A common misreading is that all the primes multiplied together, plus 1, is always prime. It is not. 2 × 3 × 5 × 7 × 11 × 13 + 1 = 30,031, which is 59 × 509. The proof only needs it to contain some new prime, and neither 59 nor 509 was on the list.

Euclid himself phrased it more cautiously: there are more primes than any given collection of them. Mathematicians now know of at least 200 different proofs of the same fact.

cards.title: Some infinities are bigger
cards.text: Georg Cantor showed that you cannot list all the real numbers, even with an infinitely long list. Whatever list you make, he could build a number that differs from the first entry in its first digit, the second entry in its second digit, and so on. So there are more real numbers than counting numbers.
cards.author: Georg Cantor
cards.source: Über eine elementare Frage der Mannigfaltigkeitslehre (1891)
cards.more:
This diagonal argument shocked mathematicians. Before Cantor, infinity was simply infinity. After him there was a hierarchy: the countable infinity of 1, 2, 3 and so on, and larger, uncountable ones like the points on a line.

The same trick, building something that disagrees with every item on a list, later powered Gödel's incompleteness theorems and Alan Turing's proof that some problems cannot be solved by any computer.

Cantor faced fierce opposition in his lifetime, notably from Leopold Kronecker. David Hilbert later defended him, declaring that no one would drive mathematicians out of the paradise Cantor had created.

cards.title: The hotel that's full but has room
cards.text: Picture a hotel with infinitely many rooms, every one occupied. A new guest arrives. No problem: move each guest from room n to room n + 1, and room 1 is free. Even infinitely many new guests fit: move everyone to room 2n, and all the odd rooms open up.
cards.author: David Hilbert
cards.source: Lecture 'Über das Unendliche' (1924-25); popularised in George Gamow, One Two Three... Infinity (1947)
cards.more:
Hilbert used the story to show how differently infinite sets behave from finite ones. In a finite hotel, full means no more guests. In an infinite one, the guests can be matched one-to-one with only some of the rooms, which is one way of defining what infinite means.

The hotel can even absorb infinitely many coaches, each with infinitely many passengers, using a clever numbering scheme. What it cannot do is give a room to one guest for every real number. That is the bigger infinity from the Cantor card, and no room plan will fit them all.

The paradox is not a contradiction. It is a reminder that intuitions built on finite things do not automatically scale up.

cards.title: Symmetry means something is conserved
cards.text: Emmy Noether proved that every continuous symmetry in physics comes with a conservation law. If the laws of physics are the same tomorrow as today, energy is conserved. If they are the same here as over there, momentum is conserved. Her 1918 theorem is a pillar of modern physics.
cards.author: Emmy Noether
cards.source: Invariante Variationsprobleme (1918)
cards.more:
Before Noether, conservation laws were facts found by experiment. After her, they followed from symmetries, which are often easier to spot. Rotational symmetry, the laws being the same in every direction, gives conservation of angular momentum.
