She did this work while barred from a proper paid post at Göttingen because she was a woman. David Hilbert and Felix Klein brought her in to help with problems in Einstein's general relativity, and for a while her lectures had to be advertised under Hilbert's name.

She went on to reshape abstract algebra. When she died in 1935, Einstein wrote that she was the most significant creative mathematical genius since the higher education of women began.

cards.title: True but unprovable
cards.text: In 1931, Kurt Gödel, then in his mid-twenties, proved that any consistent set of axioms strong enough to do basic arithmetic leaves some true statements it cannot prove. Mathematics cannot be wrapped up in one complete rulebook.
cards.author: Kurt Gödel
cards.source: On Formally Undecidable Propositions of Principia Mathematica and Related Systems (1931)
cards.more:
Gödel's trick was to make arithmetic talk about itself. He encoded statements as numbers, then built one that says, roughly, 'this statement cannot be proved in this system'. If the system could prove it, it would be proving something false. So if the system is consistent, the statement is true and unprovable.

His second theorem adds that such a system cannot prove its own consistency. Together they ended David Hilbert's hope for a complete, provably safe foundation for all of mathematics.

The theorems are often stretched to make claims about minds, religion or law. Be wary: they apply to formal systems with precise rules, not to everything that happens to be complicated.

cards.title: A rather dull taxi number
cards.text: Visiting Srinivasa Ramanujan in hospital, G. H. Hardy remarked that his taxi's number, 1729, seemed rather dull. Ramanujan disagreed at once: it is the smallest number that can be written as the sum of two cubes in two different ways. 1729 = 1³ + 12³ = 9³ + 10³.
cards.source: G. H. Hardy's recollection of a visit to Ramanujan in Putney, London (c. 1918)
cards.more:
Ramanujan grew up in southern India with little formal training in advanced mathematics. In 1913 he began writing to Hardy at Cambridge, sending pages of startling formulas. Hardy saw that the work was extraordinary and arranged for him to come to England.

The taxi story stuck because it captures his close, personal familiarity with numbers, though 1729 was not a lucky guess: it already appeared in one of his notebooks, and the French mathematician Frénicle de Bessy had noted it in 1657. Numbers like it are now called taxicab numbers.

Ramanujan died in 1920, aged 32. His notebooks are still yielding results, and ideas like his mock theta functions opened whole new areas of research.

cards.title: Seven bridges, no route
cards.text: The city of Königsberg had seven bridges linking two islands and the riverbanks. Could you take a walk crossing each bridge exactly once? In 1736 Leonhard Euler proved you could not, and in doing so laid the foundations of graph theory, the maths behind networks and route planning.
cards.source: Euler, Solutio problematis ad geometriam situs pertinentis (presented 1736)
cards.more:
Euler's leap was to throw away everything irrelevant: the shapes of the land, the lengths of the bridges, the distances. All that mattered was which pieces of land connected to which. That turns the map into dots and lines, what we now call a graph.

Then the argument is simple. Every time you pass through a piece of land you use two bridges, one in and one out. So apart from where you start and finish, every piece of land needs an even number of bridges. In Königsberg all four had an odd number, so no such walk exists.

The same abstraction now plans delivery routes, maps social networks and finds directions on your phone.

cards.title: The margin was too small
cards.text: Around 1637, Pierre de Fermat wrote in the margin of a book that no whole numbers satisfy aⁿ + bⁿ = cⁿ for any n above 2, and that he had a marvellous proof the margin was too narrow to contain. Mathematicians tried for 358 years. Andrew Wiles finally proved it in 1994.
cards.source: Fermat's note in his copy of Diophantus's Arithmetica (c. 1637); Wiles, Annals of Mathematics (1995)
cards.more:
Fermat almost certainly did not have a valid proof. The tools Wiles used, from the theory of elliptic curves and modular forms, did not exist in Fermat's time.

Wiles worked on it largely in secret for about seven years. The proof he announced in 1993 turned out to have a gap, and fixing it took another year, partly with help from his former student Richard Taylor. The full proof was published in 1995.

The theorem itself has few practical uses. Its value lay in what people built while chasing it: whole branches of number theory grew out of failed attempts, and Wiles's proof connected areas of mathematics that had seemed unrelated.

cards.title: Add up 1 to 100, fast
cards.text: Can you add up all the whole numbers from 1 to 100 in your head in under a minute? There is a trick that makes it almost instant. Try to find it before opening the answer.
cards.source: Carl Friedrich Gauss, popular schoolroom story
cards.more:
The answer is 5,050. Pair the numbers from the outside in: 1 + 100 = 101, 2 + 99 = 101, 3 + 98 = 101, and so on. There are 50 such pairs, so the total is 50 × 101.

The same idea gives a general formula: the sum of the numbers from 1 to n is n(n + 1)/2.

The trick is famously credited to a young Carl Friedrich Gauss, said to have stunned his teacher with the answer. The story comes from later retellings and has grown along the way, so treat the details as legend. The method is real, though, and so is the lesson: before grinding through a calculation, look for structure.

cards.title: Is 0.999... equal to 1?
cards.text: Write a decimal point followed by nines that go on forever. Is that number a tiny bit less than 1, or is it exactly 1?
cards.source: 0.999..., standard result in real analysis
cards.more:
It is exactly 1. One quick argument: 1/3 = 0.333..., and three times that is 0.999..., but three times 1/3 is 1.

Another: if 0.999... were less than 1, there would be a gap between them. But name any gap, however tiny, and after enough nines the number is closer to 1 than that. The only gap smaller than every positive amount is zero.

The discomfort comes from picturing the nines as a process that never finishes. In mathematics, 0.999... names the limit of 0.9, 0.99, 0.999 and so on, and that limit is 1. Plenty of numbers have two decimal spellings: 0.5 can also be written 0.4999...

cards.title: Two speeds of thought
cards.text: Daniel Kahneman describes two modes of thinking. System 1 is fast, automatic and effortless: it reads a face and finishes 2 + 2. System 2 is slow and deliberate: it works out 17 × 24. Most of the time System 1 runs the show, and System 2 signs off on its answers without checking.
cards.author: Daniel Kahneman
cards.source: Thinking, Fast and Slow, part I (2011)
cards.more:
Kahneman is clear that the two systems are characters in a story, not two places in the brain. The labels came from psychologists Keith Stanovich and Richard West; Kahneman made them famous.

The point is not that fast thinking is bad. It gets almost everything right, which is exactly why we trust it when it is wrong. Its errors cluster in predictable places: numbers, probabilities, unfamiliar situations, and anything where a vivid story is easier than the boring statistics.

The rest of this thread walks through those predictable places. The habit to build is small: notice when an answer arrived suspiciously fast on a question that deserved a slow one.

thread.title: Your brain's shortcuts in 7 cards

cards.title: A spinning wheel moved their answers
cards.text: In a classic study, people watched a wheel of fortune stop on 10 or 65, then estimated the share of African countries in the UN. Those who saw 10 guessed 25% on average. Those who saw 65 guessed 45%. A number with nothing to do with the question dragged their answers toward it.
cards.source: Tversky & Kahneman, Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases, Science (1974)
cards.more:
This is anchoring. When we estimate, we start from whatever number is lying around and adjust, and we usually adjust too little. Anchoring is one of the sturdiest findings in psychology and replicated strongly in the large Many Labs project in 2014, though studies using obviously random anchors, like a visible dice roll, have found weaker effects.

You meet anchors constantly: the first price in a negotiation, the 'was $200' on a sale tag, a manager's guess in a planning meeting before anyone else speaks.

Two counter-moves help. Write down your own estimate before you see anyone else's number. And when an anchor is on the table, deliberately argue for a value far from it before settling.

thread.title: Your brain's shortcuts in 7 cards

cards.title: The letter K trick
cards.text: Are there more English words that start with K, or that have K as the third letter? Most people say start with K, because those words are easier to think of. In fact K turns up in third place more often: ask, like, make, take. How easily examples come to mind is not a measure of how common they are.
cards.source: Tversky & Kahneman, Availability: A heuristic for judging frequency and probability, Cognitive Psychology (1973)
cards.more:
This is the availability heuristic: we judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind. Usually that works, because common things are easier to recall. But plenty of things are memorable for reasons that have nothing to do with frequency.

Plane crashes, shark attacks and dramatic crimes are vivid and heavily covered, so they feel more common than quiet killers like heart disease. One recent bad experience with a supplier can outweigh years of good service in your head.

When you catch yourself saying 'this happens all the time', ask where your examples came from. If the answer is the news, your feed or one memorable story, go and find the actual count.

thread.title: Your brain's shortcuts in 7 cards

cards.text: The human understanding, when any proposition has been once laid down (either from general admission and belief, or from the pleasure it affords), forces everything else to add fresh support and confirmation...
cards.author: Francis Bacon
cards.source: Novum Organum, book I, aphorism 46 (1620; ed. Joseph Devey)
cards.more:
Bacon described confirmation bias more than three centuries before psychologists named it. Once we hold a belief, we notice the evidence that fits, explain away the evidence that does not, and feel more certain with every pass.

In the same aphorism he tells a great story. A man is shown a temple's paintings of sailors who made vows to the gods and escaped shipwreck, and is pressed to admit the power of the gods. He asks where the portraits are of those who made their vows and drowned anyway.

The fix is the same as Bacon's: go looking for the cases that would prove you wrong, and count them with the same care as the ones that prove you right.

thread.title: Your brain's shortcuts in 7 cards

cards.title: The planes that never came back
cards.text: In World War II, statistician Abraham Wald analysed damage on bombers returning from missions. The catch: every plane he could study had survived. Hits in places where returning planes showed little damage were likely the hits that brought planes down, so those were the places that needed protecting.
cards.author: Abraham Wald
cards.source: Statistical Research Group memoranda on aircraft vulnerability, Columbia University (1943)
cards.more:
This is survivorship bias: drawing conclusions from the winners because the losers are no longer around to be counted. Bacon's drowned sailors from the last card are the same idea.

It hides in everyday advice. Studying successful founders who dropped out of college tells you nothing until you also count the dropouts who failed. Old buildings seem better made partly because the badly made ones fell down. Investment funds that closed after bad years quietly vanish from performance tables.

The popular version of Wald's story is simplified; his real memos were careful statistics for estimating how vulnerable each part of a plane was. But the lesson holds: before you learn from a sample, ask what filtered it.

thread.title: Your brain's shortcuts in 7 cards

cards.title: Everyone is biased except me
cards.text: In a survey of more than 600 Americans, over 85% said they were less biased than the average American. Only one person said they were more biased. Psychologists call this the bias blind spot: we spot bias easily in other people and almost never in ourselves.
cards.source: Scopelliti et al., Management Science (2015); term coined by Pronin, Lin & Ross (2002)
cards.more:
Emily Pronin's explanation is the introspection illusion. To judge someone else, we look at their behaviour. To judge ourselves, we look inward, search our thoughts for biased motives, find none, and conclude we are fair. But biases do not show up in introspection; they work below it.

That is why reading about biases, like this thread, mostly makes people better at diagnosing their friends. Knowing a bias exists does not switch it off.

What helps is treating yourself the way you treat others: look at your track record, not your intentions. If you have underestimated every project for a year, your sincere feeling that this one is different counts for very little.

thread.title: Your brain's shortcuts in 7 cards

cards.title: Fix the process, not your brain
cards.text: Since you cannot introspect your way out of bias, change the process instead. Before a big decision, run a premortem: imagine it is a year later and the plan has failed, then have everyone write down why. Psychologist Gary Klein argues this surfaces risks people were too polite or too confident to raise.
cards.author: Gary Klein
cards.source: Performing a Project Premortem, Harvard Business Review (2007)
cards.more:
This ties the thread together. System 1 will keep anchoring, grabbing vivid examples, defending its first conclusion and ignoring the planes that never came back. You will not feel it happening. So build checks into the routine instead of relying on vigilance.

A few with decent support: write down your own estimate before hearing anyone else's. Ask what you would expect to see if you were wrong, then go and look; in experiments by Lord, Lepper and Preston, simply asking people to consider the opposite reduced biased reading of evidence. Keep a decision journal so your track record can correct your feelings.

The premortem works because it turns doubt into an assignment rather than an insult.

thread.title: Your brain's shortcuts in 7 cards

cards.text: Millions of items of the outward order are present to my senses which never properly enter into my experience. Why? Because they have no interest for me. My experience is what I agree to attend to.
cards.author: William James
cards.source: The Principles of Psychology, vol. 1, ch. 11 'Attention' (1890)
cards.more:
James wrote this in 1890, long before smartphones. His point is that the world does not simply pour in. At every moment you select a sliver of what is available, and that selection, repeated day after day, becomes the texture of your life.

The modern twist is that many companies now compete to do the selecting for you. Feeds, notifications and autoplay are all bids for the 'agree' part of his sentence.

A useful test at the end of a day: what did I actually attend to, and would I have chosen it on purpose? You cannot attend to everything. You can decide more often what wins.

cards.text: Could the young but realize how soon they will become mere walking bundles of habits, they would give more heed to their conduct while in the plastic state. We are spinning our own fates, good or evil, and never to be undone.
cards.author: William James
cards.source: The Principles of Psychology, vol. 1, ch. 4 'Habit' (1890)
cards.more:
James's chapter on habit is one of the most quoted things in psychology, and it holds up well. He argues that habits are physical: repeated actions wear paths into the nervous system, and those paths make the next repetition easier.

His advice is concrete. Launch a new habit with as strong and decided a start as you can. Allow no exceptions until it is firmly rooted, because a single lapse undoes more than one success builds. And act on every good resolution at the first chance, rather than just enjoying the feeling of having resolved.

The flip side of 'never to be undone' is hopeful: the same mechanism that locks in bad habits will lock in good ones.

cards.text: I have discovered that all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber.
cards.author: Blaise Pascal
cards.source: Pensées, no. 139 (1670; trans. W. F. Trotter)
cards.more:
Pascal was writing about diversion: the way we chase games, gossip, work and ventures largely to avoid being alone with our own thoughts. He took the restlessness as a clue to how uncomfortable that solitude is.

A 2014 study led by Timothy Wilson made this vivid. Many participants left alone in a bare room for 6 to 15 minutes, with nothing to do but think, chose to give themselves a mild electric shock rather than sit quietly, even though they had earlier said they would pay to avoid it. Men were much more likely to do it than women.

You do not need Pascal's theology to take the point. Try ten minutes with no input at all, and notice how quickly you reach for something.

cards.title: Only a third replicated
cards.text: In 2015, a team of 270 researchers tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies. Of 97 originally significant results, only 36% came out significant again, and effects were on average about half as large. It became a landmark of what is now called the replication crisis.
cards.source: Open Science Collaboration, Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science, Science (2015)
cards.more:
This does not mean psychology is broken or that two-thirds of findings are false. A failed replication can come from a weak original, a weak replication, or real differences between the two studies. But it showed that a single published result, especially a small and surprising one, is weaker evidence than it looks.

The field responded with better habits: registering hypotheses before collecting data, larger samples, and many-lab replications of famous effects.

For readers, the lesson is a filter. Be more confident in findings that have been repeated by independent teams with big samples, and less confident in clever one-off studies that made great headlines.

cards.title: Two famous ideas that didn't hold up
cards.text: Ego depletion said willpower is a tank that runs dry. Power posing said standing like a superhero changes your hormones and your boldness. Both became hugely popular. In large, careful replications, both main effects largely vanished, and one of the power posing paper's own authors publicly abandoned it.
cards.source: Hagger et al., Perspectives on Psychological Science (2016); Dana Carney's public statement (2016)
cards.more:
The ego depletion replication involved 23 labs following a pre-registered protocol and found an effect close to zero. A later 36-lab project with over 3,500 participants found the same. For power posing, a larger study in 2015 found no hormone changes, and in 2016 co-author Dana Carney wrote that she no longer believed the effect was real. Amy Cuddy still argues posture can change how powerful people feel, a much smaller claim.

None of this means effort never feels tiring or posture never matters. It means the big, simple versions taught in talks and books were not supported.

A good rule: when a finding promises a dramatic change from a tiny trick, wait for the replications.

cards.title: Why a longer pain can feel better
cards.text: Volunteers held one hand in painfully cold water for 60 seconds, and the other for 60 seconds plus 30 more while the water warmed by one degree. Asked which trial to repeat, most chose the longer one. Memory judged each by its worst moment and its ending, not by the total.
cards.source: Kahneman, Fredrickson, Schreiber & Redelmeier, Psychological Science (1993)
cards.more:
This is the peak-end rule. When we remember an experience, we roughly average the most intense moment and the final moment, and largely ignore how long it lasted. Kahneman calls that second blind spot duration neglect.

Later work with colonoscopy patients found the same pattern: ending a procedure more gently made people remember it as less unpleasant, even though it lasted longer.

You can use this. End meetings, workouts, holidays and hard conversations on a good note, because the ending carries outsized weight in memory. And when you judge a past experience, remember that your memory is a highlight reel, not a full recording.

cards.title: Do the least skilled think they're best?
cards.text: The Dunning-Kruger effect is often summed up as: the less people know, the more they think they are geniuses. Is that what the research actually found?
cards.source: Kruger & Dunning, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (1999)
cards.more:
Not quite. In the 1999 studies, people scoring in the bottom quarter on tests of logic, grammar and humour placed themselves around the 62nd percentile on average, when they were really near the 12th. So they overestimated a lot, but still rated themselves only somewhat above average, not as the best.

There is also a live debate about how much of the pattern is a statistical artefact. Almost everyone rates themselves a bit above average, and when self-ratings and real scores are imperfectly correlated, regression to the mean alone produces a similar-looking chart.

The sturdy lesson is gentler: we are all poor judges of our own skill in areas we know little about, so outside feedback beats self-assessment.

cards.title: Does a marshmallow predict your future?
cards.text: Children who waited longer for a second marshmallow in the famous Stanford experiments did better years later. Does that mean a four-year-old's self-control sets the course of their life?
cards.source: Watts, Duncan & Quan, Psychological Science (2018)
cards.more:
Probably much less than the story suggests. The original follow-ups were small. In 2018, Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan and Haonan Quan ran a conceptual replication with a sample over ten times larger and far more diverse. The link to later achievement was about half the original size, and it shrank further once they accounted for family background and early cognitive ability.

That fits a simpler story: children from less secure homes have good reason to take a reward now, because promised rewards are less reliable in their lives. Other work found children wait longer when the adult has proved trustworthy.

Self-control still matters, but the test is not a destiny meter. Context and trust shape how long anyone will wait.

cards.title: Left-brained or right-brained?
cards.text: Logical people are left-brained and creative people right-brained, or so countless personality quizzes say. Is there anything to it?
cards.source: Nielsen et al., PLOS ONE (2013)
cards.more:
Some functions really are lopsided. For most people, key language areas sit in the left hemisphere, and the split-brain studies of Roger Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga in the 1960s showed the two halves can handle information differently.

But the leap to personality types does not hold. A 2013 University of Utah study analysed brain scans from more than 1,000 people and found no sign that individuals tend to be left-dominant or right-dominant overall. Creativity and logic both draw on networks spread across both hemispheres.

So if a quiz tells you which side you are, it is telling you about your self-image, not your brain.

cards.title: More words, calmer feelings
cards.text: Lisa Feldman Barrett found that people differ in emotional granularity. Some just feel bad; others can tell irritated from disappointed from anxious. More precise labels seem to help people cope, because a specific feeling points to a specific response.
cards.author: Lisa Feldman Barrett
cards.source: How Emotions Are Made (2017)
cards.more:
Barrett first noticed this in the 1990s, when some study participants used words like anxious, sad and angry almost interchangeably while others drew sharp lines between them. Research since then links higher granularity with more flexible emotion regulation, and lower granularity with conditions like depression and anxiety, although cause and effect are hard to untangle.

The practical part is easy to try. When you feel off, go one level more specific. Not 'stressed' but 'behind', 'dreading Tuesday' or 'embarrassed about that email'. Each points to a different next step.

Building vocabulary helps too: reading fiction, borrowing words from other languages, or keeping a list of feeling words nearby for a while.

cards.title: Losses hit about twice as hard
cards.text: Kahneman and Tversky showed that losing $100 feels worse than winning $100 feels good. Many people turn down a coin flip that pays $150 on heads and costs $100 on tails, even though it is a good bet. In typical studies, losses weigh roughly twice as much as equal gains.
cards.author: Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky
cards.source: Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk, Econometrica (1979)
cards.more:
Loss aversion helps explain why we hold losing investments too long, why 'don't lose your discount' can work better than 'get a discount', and why people value things more once they own them.

It is not a universal law. Later research found it weaker or absent for small stakes, and some researchers argue that effects blamed on it, like sticking with the status quo, are better explained by simple inertia. The ratio of about two is an average, not a constant.

A useful habit: when you are agonising over a choice, reframe it. Ask what you would pick if you were starting fresh with nothing to lose, and see whether the answer changes.

cards.title: The box that's already ticked
cards.text: In countries where you must opt in to be an organ donor, registered consent tends to be low. In similar countries where you must opt out, it is near universal. The question is the same; only the default changed. Doing nothing is a choice, and whoever sets the default makes it for most people.
cards.author: Eric Johnson and Daniel Goldstein
cards.source: Do Defaults Save Lives?, Science (2003)
cards.more:
Defaults work for several reasons: switching takes effort, the default feels like a recommendation, and staying put feels safer than acting. Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein built much of their book Nudge around this, and automatic enrolment in workplace pensions is one of its biggest success stories.

There is a caveat to the organ example. Actual donation rates differ far less than registration rates, because families, hospitals and infrastructure matter a lot.

In your own life, look for defaults working against you: subscriptions that renew, the phone on the desk, the snacks in sight. Then set new defaults that do the right thing when you are not thinking about it.

cards.title: They're careless, I'm just busy
cards.text: When someone cuts us off in traffic, we decide they are a selfish driver. When we do it, we know we were late and distracted. Psychologist Lee Ross named the first half of this the fundamental attribution error: we explain other people's actions by their character and underrate their circumstances.
cards.author: Lee Ross
cards.source: The Intuitive Psychologist and His Shortcomings, Advances in Experimental Social Psychology (1977)
cards.more:
The classic demonstration came in 1967. Edward Jones and Victor Harris had people read essays praising or attacking Fidel Castro. Even when readers were told the writers had been assigned their side, they still judged the writers to believe what they had argued.

The effect is real but varies. It appears weaker in cultures that pay more attention to context, and later reviews found the self-versus-others version less consistent than once thought.

It is still a good prompt. When someone annoys you, come up with one plausible situational explanation before settling on a verdict about their character. You will often be right, and you will be easier to work with either way.

cards.title: Change the story, not the face
cards.text: Psychologist James Gross compared two ways of handling emotion. Suppression means hiding what you feel. Reappraisal means changing how you interpret the situation, like reading pre-talk nerves as readiness. Reappraisal tends to work better; suppression tends to cost memory, effort and closeness with others.
cards.author: James Gross
cards.source: Gross & John, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (2003)
cards.more:
Gross's model sorts emotion regulation by timing. Reappraisal acts early, changing the meaning of a situation before the emotional response fully builds. Suppression acts late, clamping down on the expression of a feeling that is already running.

In lab studies, suppressing feelings did not reduce how bad people felt, raised physiological arousal, and impaired memory for what was happening. In daily life, people who habitually reappraise tend to report more positive emotion and closer relationships than habitual suppressors.

Reappraisal is not pretending things are fine. It is finding an interpretation that is also true and more useful: this deadline means people rely on me; this argument means we both care. Try it on something small first.

cards.text: The butcher has more meat in his shop than he himself can consume, and the brewer and the baker would each of them be willing to purchase a part of it. But they have nothing to offer in exchange... and the butcher is already provided with all the bread and beer which he has immediate occasion for.
cards.author: Adam Smith
cards.source: The Wealth of Nations, Book 1, ch. 4, Of the Origin and Use of Money (1776)
cards.more:
This is the textbook story of where money came from. Imagine a world of barter. The butcher wants nothing the baker has right now, so no trade happens. Economists later named this the problem of the double coincidence of wants: both sides have to want what the other has, at the same moment.

Smith's solution is that sensible people started keeping some commodity everyone would accept, like cattle, salt, shells or metal, and that commodity became money.

It's a tidy, logical story, and it has shaped economics for 250 years. The next card asks an awkward question: did it ever actually happen that way?

thread.title: Where money came from (8 cards)

cards.title: Debt came before money
cards.text: The anthropologist David Graeber pointed out that nobody has ever found a society that ran on everyday barter in the way the textbooks describe. Neighbours instead kept loose track of who owed whom. In his account, credit and debt came first, and coins and barter showed up later, mostly between strangers who didn't trust each other.
cards.author: David Graeber
cards.source: Debt: The First 5,000 Years (2011)
cards.more:
Graeber wasn't the first to say this. Anthropologists had long reported that barter, where it exists, tends to happen between outsiders, not between neighbours who see each other every day.

Within a village, if you need the butcher's meat now, you take it and owe him. The obligation is remembered, settled later, often in a different form. That's credit, and it needs trust and memory, not coins.

Some of the earliest writing we have from Mesopotamia, thousands of years before coins, consists of accounts and records of what people owed. Which raises the question of what those debts were measured in.

thread.title: Where money came from (8 cards)

cards.title: The shekel was a weight first
cards.text: Before it was a coin, the shekel was a unit of weight in ancient Mesopotamia. The word is attested by about 2150 BC, and the Code of Hammurabi, around 1750 BC, prices things like a year of unskilled labour in shekels of silver. Money existed as a unit of account long before anyone stamped a coin.
cards.source: Wikipedia, Shekel
cards.more:
The name comes from a Semitic root meaning to weigh, and it survives in Hebrew words for weight and for weighing. A shekel was simply a set amount of silver, weighed out on a scale.

In practice, a lot of everyday dealing in Mesopotamia didn't involve handing silver around at all. Temple and palace administrators recorded obligations in shekels, and debts could be settled in barley or other goods at an agreed rate.

That's the key shift in thinking: money is first a way of measuring and keeping score. The physical object, a lump of silver, a coin, a note, came later and was just a convenient token of that score.

thread.title: Where money came from (8 cards)

cards.title: The first coins came from Lydia
cards.text: The oldest coins we know of were made in Lydia, in what is now western Turkey, around the 7th century BC. They were stamped lumps of electrum, a natural mix of gold and silver. The stamp was the breakthrough: it promised a standard weight, so nobody had to weigh each piece.
cards.source: Wikipedia, Lydia
cards.more:
Lydia was rich in electrum, which washed down from its rivers, and its kings put that wealth to work. Herodotus later wrote that the Lydians were the first people known to have struck coins of gold and silver.

The most famous Lydian king was Croesus, whose name still means fabulously rich. He is credited with introducing coins of pure gold and pure silver, rather than the unpredictable natural alloy.

Coins spread fast through the Greek world. A stamped coin was money you could trust without a scale, as long as you trusted whoever stamped it. That question of trust is about to get much bigger.

thread.title: Where money came from (8 cards)

cards.title: Paper money was a fix for heavy coins
cards.text: The first paper money appeared in Sichuan, China, in the 11th century, during the Song dynasty. Sichuan used iron coins, which were heavy and low in value, so merchants began issuing paper notes called jiaozi instead. Within a few years merchant groups standardized them, and the government soon took over issuing them.
cards.source: Wikipedia, Jiaozi (currency)
cards.more:
The early notes were essentially receipts: deposit your iron cash, carry a slip of paper, and redeem it later. That's far easier than lugging strings of iron coins around a region of mountains and rivers.

Once the state took control, notes were printed with multiple colours and seals to fight counterfeiting, and the issuing office charged a small fee for exchanging coins into paper.

Here money becomes almost pure promise. The paper itself is worth nothing. Its value rests entirely on believing the issuer will honour it, and on not issuing too much. Later Chinese governments learned the hard way what happens when they print too freely.

thread.title: Where money came from (8 cards)

cards.title: Bad money drives out good
cards.text: Gresham's law says that when two forms of money must legally be accepted at the same face value, people hoard the more valuable one and spend the worse one. Mix full-silver coins with debased ones and the good coins vanish into drawers and melting pots, leaving only the bad ones in circulation.
cards.author: Thomas Gresham
cards.source: Gresham's law, named by Henry Dunning Macleod in 1857 after Sir Thomas Gresham (1519-1579)
cards.more:
Gresham was a Tudor financier who advised Elizabeth I after her father, Henry VIII, had badly debased England's coinage. But he didn't discover the idea. Nicole Oresme and Nicolaus Copernicus described it, and the comic playwright Aristophanes joked about the same effect in ancient Athens.

The law is really about incentives. If the state says a coin with half the silver is worth the same as a full one, nobody sensible pays with the full one.

It also shows why debasement tempts rulers. Shaving metal from each coin lets a government spend more without raising taxes, quietly passing the cost to everyone holding money. Which leads to Keynes.

thread.title: Where money came from (8 cards)

cards.text: There is no subtler, no surer means of overturning the existing basis of society than to debauch the currency. The process engages all the hidden forces of economic law on the side of destruction, and does it in a manner which not one man in a million is able to diagnose.
cards.author: John Maynard Keynes
cards.source: The Economic Consequences of the Peace, ch. 6 (1919)
cards.more:
Keynes wrote this in 1919, after resigning from the British delegation at the Paris peace talks in protest at the reparations being imposed on Germany. A few lines earlier he notes that Lenin is said to have called debauching the currency the best way to destroy capitalism.

His point is that inflation is a hidden tax and a hidden transfer. Through it, governments can confiscate, secretly and unobserved, a large part of their citizens' wealth, enriching some and ruining others, while everyone blames speculators.

Within four years Germany was in hyperinflation. The whole history in this thread comes down to this: money works only while people trust it.

thread.title: Where money came from (8 cards)

cards.title: Money is a story we all believe
cards.text: Yuval Noah Harari calls money the most universal and efficient system of mutual trust ever invented. A banknote or a number in an app has almost no value in itself. It works because everyone believes everyone else will accept it, including strangers who share nothing else, not even a language or a religion.
cards.author: Yuval Noah Harari
cards.source: Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind, ch. 10 (English edition, 2014)
cards.more:
This ties the whole thread together. Smith imagined money as a handy commodity. Graeber showed debts and trust came first. Mesopotamian scribes kept score in shekels of silver. Lydian kings stamped their guarantee on metal. Song China made it paper. Gresham and Keynes showed what happens when that trust is abused.

At every stage, the thing that mattered was not the object but the shared belief behind it. Most money today is not even paper. It's entries in bank databases.

Harari's twist is that money isn't less real because it's imagined. Shared stories, like money, laws and nations, are exactly what let millions of strangers cooperate.

thread.title: Where money came from (8 cards)

cards.text: It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest.
cards.author: Adam Smith
cards.source: The Wealth of Nations, Book 1, ch. 2 (1776)
cards.more:
This is probably the most quoted line in economics, and it's often misread as greed is good. Smith's point is narrower and more interesting. Trade lets strangers serve each other without needing to be friends. The baker doesn't have to love you. He just has to want your money, and you his bread.

The next sentence matters: we address ourselves, he says, not to their humanity but to their self-love, and talk of their advantages, not our needs.

Smith also wrote a whole book, The Theory of Moral Sentiments, on sympathy and conscience. He didn't think people were only selfish. He thought markets work even when they are.

cards.text: People of the same trade seldom meet together, even for merriment and diversion, but the conversation ends in a conspiracy against the public, or in some contrivance to raise prices.
cards.author: Adam Smith
cards.source: The Wealth of Nations, Book 1, ch. 10 (1776)
cards.more:
People who think of Adam Smith as a cheerleader for business are often surprised by this line. Smith was deeply suspicious of merchants and manufacturers whenever they could escape competition. He saw them lobbying for monopolies, tariffs and guild privileges, all at the public's expense.

He was realistic about the fix, too. In the very next sentence he admits that such meetings can't be banned without trampling liberty. His argument is that the law should at least not make them easier, for example by requiring traders to register together.

Modern antitrust law grew out of the same worry: competitors cooperating to raise prices.

cards.text: ...the cost of a thing is the amount of what I will call life which is required to be exchanged for it, immediately or in the long run.
cards.author: Henry David Thoreau
cards.source: Walden, ch. 1, Economy (1854)
cards.more:
Thoreau applies this straight away to houses. An average house near Concord cost about eight hundred dollars, he says, and saving that much would take a labourer ten to fifteen years of his life. Was the house worth fifteen years?

It's a powerful way to reframe a price tag. Divide the cost of anything by what you earn per hour, after tax, and you get the hours of your life it really costs.

Thoreau's opening chapter of Walden is called Economy for a reason. Long before personal finance blogs, he was tracking every expense of his cabin down to the half cent, to see how little he actually needed.

cards.text: Men, it has been well said, think in herds; it will be seen that they go mad in herds, while they only recover their senses slowly, and one by one.
cards.author: Charles Mackay
cards.source: Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds, Preface (1841)
cards.more:
Mackay's book covers financial manias like the Mississippi Company scheme in France and the South Sea Bubble in Britain, both of which collapsed in 1720, and the Dutch tulip craze of the 1630s.

Historians now think he exaggerated some of it. Research by Anne Goldgar suggests tulip mania was a much smaller affair than his colourful account, with few documented ruinations. Mackay relied heavily on moralizing pamphlets.

But his central observation has held up through every boom since, from railway shares to dot-com stocks to crypto. Enthusiasm spreads socially and fast. Sobering up is a lonely process, one investor at a time.

cards.title: Wealth is what you don't see
cards.text: Morgan Housel points out that spending is visible and wealth isn't. When you see someone in an expensive car, the only thing you know for sure is that they have less money than before they bought it. Real wealth is the cars not bought, the money not spent, sitting quietly where nobody can see it.
cards.author: Morgan Housel
cards.source: The Psychology of Money, ch. 9 (2020)
cards.more:
This creates a trap. We learn what being rich looks like by watching what rich people buy, but the things they didn't buy are invisible. So we copy the spending, not the saving.

Housel makes a related point he calls the man in the car paradox. When people see someone in a flashy car, they rarely think about the driver. They imagine themselves in it. The admiration the buyer hoped for mostly goes to the car.

His advice is not to never spend. It's to recognize that wealth is optionality: savings that give you choices later, rather than possessions that signal status now.

cards.title: Never trust advice without skin in the game
cards.text: Nassim Taleb argues you should be wary of anyone who gets the upside of a decision while someone else bears the downside. Bankers paid bonuses for risks that blow up on taxpayers, or pundits who are never penalized for bad forecasts, have every reason to keep making the same mistakes.
cards.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
cards.source: Skin in the Game (2018)
cards.more:
Taleb likes to cite one of the oldest examples on record: the Code of Hammurabi, almost 4,000 years old. If a builder's house collapsed and killed its owner, the builder was put to death. Harsh, but it made sure the person with the most knowledge about the risk also carried it.

His point isn't about punishment. It's about feedback. When people pay for their own mistakes, they learn, or they leave the field. When they don't, bad judgment survives and spreads.

A useful habit from the book: before taking advice, ask what the adviser loses if they're wrong. If the answer is nothing, weigh the advice accordingly.

cards.title: When a number becomes a goal
cards.text: Charles Goodhart observed that any statistic used to steer policy tends to stop behaving reliably once people start managing toward it. Make a measure the target, and people will find ways to hit the number without delivering the thing the number was supposed to show.
cards.author: Charles Goodhart
cards.source: Problems of Monetary Management: The UK Experience (1975)
cards.more:
Goodhart, an economist at the Bank of England, was writing about money supply figures. When the government targeted a particular measure of money, the financial system shifted its behaviour, and the measure stopped tracking what policymakers cared about.

The anthropologist Marilyn Strathern later put it in the snappy general form people now quote, and the idea turned out to apply almost everywhere. Hospitals measured on waiting times, schools judged on test scores, programmers paid by lines of code, call centres timed by call length.

The lesson isn't to stop measuring. It's to watch for gaming, rotate measures, and never forget the goal behind the number.

cards.title: Losses hurt more than gains feel good
cards.text: Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky found that people feel a loss much more sharply than an equal gain. Offered a coin flip that wins 150 dollars or loses 100, most people refuse, even though the odds favour them. Losses loom roughly one and a half to two and a half times larger.
cards.author: Daniel Kahneman
cards.source: Thinking, Fast and Slow, part 4 (2011); Kahneman and Tversky, Prospect Theory (1979)
cards.more:
Loss aversion was a central piece of prospect theory, published by Kahneman and Tversky in 1979, work that later earned Kahneman the Nobel prize in economics. Tversky died before it was awarded.

It explains a lot of everyday behaviour. Investors hang on to losing stocks to avoid making the loss real. Shoppers respond more to avoiding a fee than to an equivalent discount. Negotiators fight harder to avoid giving something up than to gain something new.

Knowing about the bias doesn't make it disappear, but it helps. A good check is to ask whether you'd make the same choice if it were framed as a gain instead of a loss.

cards.title: Trade pays even if you're worse at everything
cards.text: David Ricardo showed that two countries can both gain from trade even if one is better at producing everything. What matters is comparative advantage: each should specialize in what it gives up least to make. His example had Portugal making both wine and cloth more cheaply than England, yet both still gained by trading.
cards.author: David Ricardo
cards.source: On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, ch. 7 (1817)
cards.more:
In Ricardo's numbers, Portugal needs 80 workers a year to make a batch of wine and 90 for cloth. England needs 120 for wine and 100 for cloth. Portugal is better at both. But it's much better at wine, so it should make wine and buy cloth, while England does the reverse, and both end up with more.

The same logic works for people. A brilliant lawyer who types faster than her assistant should still hand over the typing, because her time is worth far more doing law.

Comparative advantage is one of the least intuitive ideas in economics, and one of the most robust.

cards.title: The great Hanoi rat bounty
cards.text: In 1902 the French colonial government in Hanoi, fearing plague, paid a bounty of one cent for every rat tail handed in. Hundreds of thousands of rats were killed. Then officials started noticing live rats running around without tails. People were cutting off the tails and letting the rats go free to breed.
cards.source: Wikipedia, Great Hanoi Rat Massacre (citing historian Michael Vann)
cards.more:
The authorities had paid for a proxy, tails, rather than the thing they wanted, fewer rats. A tailless rat that goes on breeding produces more future tails, so the scheme gave people a reason to keep the rat population going. There were reports of rat farming too.

The bounty was eventually cancelled, and other anti-plague measures were tried instead.

Economists call this a perverse incentive, and it's a perfect real-world example of Goodhart's law. A similar tale about a cobra bounty in British India is often told, but the Hanoi case is the one with solid documentation, thanks to the historian Michael Vann's work in colonial archives.

cards.title: The king who moved the price of gold
cards.text: In 1324 Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire, passed through Cairo on pilgrimage to Mecca and gave away so much gold that, according to the historian al-Umari, its value in Egypt dropped. A measure of gold that had been worth 25 silver dirhams fell below 22, and stayed there for at least twelve years.
cards.source: Al-Umari, as cited in Wikipedia, Mansa Musa
cards.more:
Mali controlled some of the richest gold sources of the medieval world, and Musa travelled with an enormous entourage and a vast supply of gold. His visit made Mali famous across the Muslim world and onto European maps.

The story is often inflated online into Musa single-handedly wrecking Egypt's economy. The historian Warren Schultz argues the drop was within normal price swings of the period, so treat the dramatic version with care.

There's a twist, too. Musa apparently ran short on the way home and borrowed from Cairo merchants. Even the richest man around can spend faster than he plans.

cards.title: The bat and the ball
cards.text: A bat and a ball cost 1.10 dollars in total. The bat costs 1.00 dollar more than the ball. How much does the ball cost? Answer quickly, then check.
cards.source: Shane Frederick, Cognitive Reflection and Decision Making, Journal of Economic Perspectives (2005)
cards.more:
Five cents. The answer that jumps to mind is ten cents, but then the bat would cost 1.10 and the total would be 1.20. With a 5 cent ball and a 1.05 dollar bat, the total is 1.10 and the difference is exactly one dollar.

The puzzle comes from Shane Frederick's Cognitive Reflection Test, and Daniel Kahneman made it famous in Thinking, Fast and Slow. Many students at top universities get it wrong, not because the math is hard, but because a quick, confident answer arrives first and nobody checks it.

It's a small lesson with big uses in money decisions: the fast answer feels right, so it rarely gets questioned.

cards.title: Grains on a chessboard
cards.text: Put one grain of wheat on the first square of a chessboard, two on the second, four on the third, doubling each time. Roughly how many grains will be on the whole board?
cards.source: Wikipedia, Wheat and chessboard problem
cards.more:
18,446,744,073,709,551,615, which is 2 to the power of 64, minus one. That's more than 18 quintillion grains, far more wheat than humanity has ever grown.

The legend says the inventor of chess asked a king for this reward, and the king laughed at how modest it seemed. The first half of the board is manageable. The first 32 squares hold about four billion grains in total. The second half is where things explode.

That's the shape of compound growth, whether in savings, debt or a pandemic. Early on it looks like nothing. Most of the action comes at the end, which is why starting early, or stopping early, matters so much.

cards.title: Evolution in three ingredients
cards.text: Darwin's core argument needs just three ingredients. Individuals vary. Much of that variation is inherited. And far more offspring are born than can survive. Put those together, and traits that help survival and reproduction become more common, generation after generation. He called it natural selection.
cards.author: Charles Darwin
cards.source: On the Origin of Species, ch. 4 (1859)
cards.more:
None of the three ingredients was controversial on its own. Breeders knew animals vary and pass traits to their young, and Thomas Malthus had written about populations outgrowing their food supply. Darwin's leap, reached independently by Alfred Russel Wallace, was to see what happens when all three act together over immense spans of time. Their ideas were first presented jointly in 1858.

No goal or designer is required. Selection simply filters each generation, keeping what works a little better in that place and time. This thread walks through the idea step by step: the pressure behind it, evidence of it happening before our eyes, and what it tells us about all life on Earth.

thread.title: How evolution works, step by step (7 cards)

cards.text: The elephant is reckoned to be the slowest breeder of all known animals... if this be so, at the end of the fifth century there would be alive fifteen million elephants, descended from the first pair.
cards.author: Charles Darwin
cards.source: On the Origin of Species, ch. 3 (1859)
cards.more:
This is the pressure behind natural selection, made vivid. Every species can multiply far faster than its world can support. Darwin picked the elephant on purpose, the slowest breeder he knew of, and even it would overrun the planet if nothing held it back. In later editions he reworked the arithmetic and arrived at nearly nineteen million elephants after about 750 years, but the point stands.

Elephant numbers don't actually explode. So most offspring of every species must die before reproducing, from hunger, predators, disease or bad luck. Darwin called this the struggle for existence. Because so many don't make it, any small inherited edge changes who gets to become a parent.

thread.title: How evolution works, step by step (7 cards)

cards.title: Moths that changed colour with the soot
cards.text: Peppered moths are usually pale and speckled, hidden against lichen-covered bark. As soot from the Industrial Revolution blackened England's trees, a rare dark form spread. Around Manchester, dark moths made up 98 percent of records by 1895. When clean-air laws took effect, the pale form came back.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Peppered moth evolution
cards.more:
Birds hunt moths by sight. On pale bark, dark moths stood out and were eaten; on soot-darkened bark, the pale ones did. The variation already existed, colour was inherited, and the environment shifted which version survived. That's natural selection, visible within a human lifetime.

Bernard Kettlewell studied the mechanism between 1953 and 1956, and his experiments were later attacked, even accused of fraud. So the geneticist Michael Majerus ran a meticulous seven-year study starting in 2001, published after his death in 2012. It vindicated Kettlewell in detail. The dark form's rise and fall remains one of the clearest examples of evolution in action.

thread.title: How evolution works, step by step (7 cards)

cards.title: Evolution measured in two years
cards.text: Since 1973, Peter and Rosemary Grant have studied Darwin's finches on the tiny Galápagos island of Daphne Major. In 1977 a drought left mostly large, tough seeds. Many finches died, and the birds that followed had measurably larger beaks. Selection had acted within a couple of years.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Peter and Rosemary Grant; Darwin's finches
cards.more:
Darwin assumed natural selection was too slow to watch. The Grants proved otherwise by catching, tagging, measuring and taking blood samples from finches on the island, spending six months of every year there for decades. In the 1977 rainy season only 24 millimetres of rain fell. Small, soft seeds ran out, and birds with bigger beaks, able to crack the hard ones, survived and bred.

The effect can also run in reverse. After a drought in 2003, with a larger competing finch species now on the island, the medium ground finch's average beak size went down instead. Evolution isn't a march toward bigger or better. It tracks whatever the environment rewards right now.

thread.title: How evolution works, step by step (7 cards)

cards.title: Whales once walked on land
cards.text: Whales descend from four-legged land mammals. Around 50 million years ago, in what is now South Asia, wolf-like animals such as Pakicetus lived in and around water. Over millions of years their descendants became fully aquatic. The closest living relatives of whales are hippos.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Evolution of cetaceans; Pakicetus
cards.more:
Whale evolution is one of the best-documented transitions in the fossil record, running from Pakicetus at the water's edge, through Ambulocetus, whose name means walking whale, to fully marine forms whose hind limbs had shrunk away.

Traces remain in living whales. Many still carry small pelvic bones, leftovers of their ancestors' hips, now hidden deep inside the body and repurposed to support reproductive organs. And molecular studies, entirely independent of the fossils, place whales among the even-toed hoofed mammals, sharing a common ancestor with hippos that lived around 55 million years ago. Bones and genes, two separate lines of evidence, tell the same story.

thread.title: How evolution works, step by step (7 cards)

cards.title: Every living thing shares one code
cards.text: Bacteria, mushrooms, oak trees and you all read DNA using nearly the same genetic code: a table of 64 three-letter codons that map to the same amino acids. That's why bacteria can be engineered to make human insulin, which has been produced this way for medical use since 1982.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Genetic code; Insulin (medication)
cards.more:
There's no obvious reason the code had to be this way. Francis Crick suggested it may be a frozen accident: fixed very early, then locked in, because changing it would scramble almost every protein a cell makes. The fact that nearly all life shares it, with only minor variations, is powerful evidence that all of it descends from a single shared ancestor.

Biologists call that ancestor LUCA, the last universal common ancestor. Most studies suggest it lived at least 3.5 billion years ago, and possibly earlier. Every organism alive today, from the finches on Daphne Major to the bacteria in your gut, is a distant cousin through it.

thread.title: How evolution works, step by step (7 cards)

cards.text: There is grandeur in this view of life, with its several powers, having been originally breathed into a few forms or into one; and that, whilst this planet has gone cycling on according to the fixed law of gravity, from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved.
cards.author: Charles Darwin
cards.source: On the Origin of Species, ch. 14 (1859)
cards.more:
These are the final words of the first edition of the Origin. Notice the end of the sentence: have been, and are being, evolved. Darwin understood that evolution isn't only ancient history. It is happening now, as the moths and finches in this thread show.

The whole thread in one breath: living things vary, much of that variation is inherited, far more are born than can survive, and so the environment keeps editing every species. Given enough time, that simple process links whales to hippos, and you to every other living thing through one shared genetic code. Darwin saw grandeur in that rather than loss. It's hard to disagree.

thread.title: How evolution works, step by step (7 cards)

cards.text: When we try to pick out anything by itself, we find it hitched to everything else in the universe.
cards.author: John Muir
cards.source: My First Summer in the Sierra, ch. 6 (1911)
cards.more:
In 1869, a young John Muir spent a summer in California's Sierra Nevada, working alongside a flock of sheep being driven to mountain pastures. His journal from those months became this book, published in 1911, and it brims with giddy delight at rocks, flowers, insects, storms and light.

This line is often passed around in looser paraphrased versions; this is how he actually wrote it. It captures the heart of what we now call ecology: a flower depends on its pollinators, which depend on the weather, which depends on the mountains. Muir went on to co-found the Sierra Club and became one of the most influential champions of national parks.

cards.text: Hence, both in space and time, we seem to be brought somewhat near to that great fact—that mystery of mysteries—the first appearance of new beings on this earth.
cards.author: Charles Darwin
cards.source: The Voyage of the Beagle, ch. 17 (2nd ed., 1845)
cards.more:
Darwin wrote this about the Galápagos Islands, which HMS Beagle reached in September 1835. He was struck that such young volcanic islands, with craters and lava flows still sharp, held so many creatures found nowhere else. New species seemed to have appeared there, geologically speaking, quite recently.

The phrase mystery of mysteries was borrowed. The astronomer John Herschel had used it in an 1836 letter to the geologist Charles Lyell, about how extinct species come to be replaced by new ones. In the opening of On the Origin of Species, Darwin credits it to one of our greatest philosophers, meaning Herschel. The Origin, published 24 years after this visit, was his answer.

cards.text: Heaven is under our feet as well as over our heads.
cards.author: Henry David Thoreau
cards.source: Walden, ch. 16, The Pond in Winter (1854)
cards.more:
Thoreau wrote this after cutting through a foot of snow and a foot of ice on Walden Pond in winter. Kneeling to drink, he looked down into what he called the quiet parlor of the fishes, softly lit as if through ground glass, its sandy floor the same as in summer.

In the same chapter he did something very practical. Some people said Walden Pond was bottomless, so he sounded it with a cod-line and a stone, and found its greatest depth was exactly one hundred and two feet. It is a nice pairing: the man who found heaven in a frozen pond also took the trouble to measure it. Wonder and careful observation are not opposites.

cards.title: The animals that survived open space
cards.text: Tardigrades, or water bears, are tiny eight-legged animals. In 2007, dried-out tardigrades rode outside a spacecraft for 10 days, exposed to the vacuum of space. Vacuum alone had no significant effect on them. Rehydrated back on Earth, they revived and went on laying eggs.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Tardigrade (FOTON-M3 mission)
cards.more:
Their trick is a state called the tun. When the moss or pond they live in dries out, tardigrades draw in their legs and lose almost all their water, and their metabolism stops. In that state they can endure conditions that would kill nearly anything else, then revive when water returns.

They aren't invincible. In the same experiment, adding the full blast of unfiltered solar ultraviolet light killed most of them, though a few still recovered. But for a complex animal with a brain and muscles to shrug off the vacuum of space is remarkable. Tardigrades live almost everywhere, from mountaintops to the deep sea. On mosses they can reach over 2 million per square metre.

cards.title: The shark that may be 400 years old
cards.text: Greenland sharks may be the longest-lived animals with a backbone. Radiocarbon dating of their eye lenses suggests they live at least 272 years, and the oldest one studied was estimated at 392 years, give or take 120. They don't reach maturity until around age 150.
cards.source: Nielsen et al., Science (2016); Wikipedia: Greenland shark
cards.more:
Sharks have no bony parts that lay down neat yearly rings, so their age was long a mystery. The breakthrough came in 2016, when researchers dated tissue in the core of the eye lens, which forms during development and doesn't change afterwards. Measuring its carbon-14, including the spike left by nuclear bomb tests in the 1950s and 60s, let them estimate when each shark was born.

Greenland sharks live in the cold North Atlantic and Arctic, can grow over 6 metres long, and lead slow lives. The uncertainty on the oldest estimate is wide, but even the low end means some sharks alive today were born before Charles Darwin.

cards.title: Your body's busiest factory
cards.text: An adult human makes about 2.4 million new red blood cells every second. Each one circulates for roughly 100 to 120 days before being recycled. At any moment you carry some 20 to 30 trillion of them, making them by far the most numerous cells in your body.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Red blood cell
cards.more:
Red blood cells are stripped-down specialists. As they mature in the bone marrow, they lose their nucleus and most of their internal machinery to make room for haemoglobin, the iron-rich protein that carries oxygen. One way to picture them is as flexible little sacks of haemoglobin. Without a nucleus they can't divide or repair themselves, which is why they need constant replacing.

They are also constantly on the move. A typical red blood cell makes a full circuit of your body in about a minute. Over a life of three to four months, that adds up to well over a hundred thousand round trips through your heart, lungs and every other tissue.

cards.title: You are not mostly bacteria
cards.text: A popular claim says bacteria in your body outnumber your own cells ten to one. A careful 2016 recount found the real ratio is much closer to one to one: roughly 38 trillion bacteria to 30 trillion human cells, for a typical adult man.
cards.source: Sender, Fuchs and Milo, PLoS Biology and Cell (2016); Wikipedia: Human microbiome
cards.more:
The ten-to-one figure traced back to rough estimates from the 1970s that got repeated for decades without being checked. When Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo at the Weizmann Institute redid the sums with modern data, the ratio collapsed. Their count of human cells is dominated by blood cells, which make up about 90 percent of the total.

By weight, your bacteria are modest: about 0.2 kilograms. But numbers aren't the whole story. Your microbes, most of them living in your gut, help digest food, train your immune system and crowd out harmful invaders. You are not mostly bacteria, but you are certainly not alone.

cards.title: A tree older than the pyramids
cards.text: A Great Basin bristlecone pine called Methuselah began growing around 2833 BC, making it more than 4,850 years old. It is credited as the oldest known living non-clonal organism on Earth. It was already centuries old when the Great Pyramid of Giza was finished.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Pinus longaeva
cards.more:
Bristlecones grow high in the mountains of the western United States, in cold, dry, harsh conditions, and that's part of their secret. They grow incredibly slowly, producing dense, resinous wood. As an old tree ages, much of its living tissue can die back, until only a narrow strip of bark connects the roots to a few living branches, and the tree carries on.

Tree ages like this are counted from growth rings in thin cores drilled out of the trunk. Non-clonal matters here: some clonal colonies, like aspen groves joined by one root system, may be older, but Methuselah is a single tree that has stood on its own since the Bronze Age.

cards.title: Bees give directions by dancing
cards.text: A honeybee that finds good flowers returns to the hive and performs a waggle dance. The angle of her waggle run, measured from straight up on the comb, matches the direction of the food relative to the Sun. How long she waggles tells how far away it is.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Waggle dance; Karl von Frisch
cards.more:
Karl von Frisch, an Austrian scientist, was one of the first to decode this language, through years of patient experiments with marked bees and feeding stations. He shared the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his work on animal behaviour.

The system is elegant. Inside the dark hive, the comb hangs vertically, so the bees use straight up as a stand-in for the Sun's direction. A run straight up means fly toward the Sun; a run angled to the right means fly that same angle to the right of the Sun. Other bees follow the dancer closely, then head out to find the flowers themselves.

cards.title: The bacteria living inside your cells
cards.text: Lynn Margulis championed a once-doubted idea: the mitochondria that power your cells were once free-living bacteria. Long ago, one cell engulfed another, and instead of digesting it, the two became partners. Plant chloroplasts began the same way. Every complex cell is an ancient merger.
cards.author: Lynn Margulis
cards.source: On the Origin of Mitosing Cells, Journal of Theoretical Biology (1967)
cards.more:
The idea, called symbiogenesis or endosymbiotic theory, had been proposed in 1905 and 1910 by the Russian botanist Konstantin Mereschkowski, but it was largely ignored. Margulis revived it in 1967 and backed it with microbiological evidence.

The clues are striking once you know to look. Mitochondria and chloroplasts carry their own small chromosomes, separate from the cell's main DNA. They reproduce by splitting in two, the way bacteria do, on their own schedule. Chloroplasts even share a double membrane and other features with free-living cyanobacteria. Today the theory is standard textbook biology, and a reminder that cooperation, not just competition, has shaped life.

cards.title: Seeing evolution from the gene's view
cards.text: Richard Dawkins suggested looking at evolution from the gene's point of view. Bodies come and go, but genes get copied across generations. Genes that happen to build bodies good at surviving and reproducing get copied more. In that sense, he argued, organisms are vehicles genes build to get themselves passed on.
cards.author: Richard Dawkins
cards.source: The Selfish Gene (1976)
cards.more:
The word selfish trips people up. Dawkins didn't mean genes have desires, or that people ought to be selfish. He meant that the genes we see today are, statistically, the ones that were good at getting copied, and that this lens explains a lot.

It helps explain why animals help their relatives: a gene that nudges you to help your siblings can spread, because siblings are likely to carry copies of the same gene. That idea, kin selection, came largely from W. D. Hamilton's work, which the book did much to popularise, along with George C. Williams's earlier thinking. The book also introduced a word you probably use: meme.

cards.title: Are you still the same body?
cards.text: Your body is constantly replacing parts of itself. Red blood cells last about four months, and roughly a tenth of your fat cells are renewed each year. Like the ancient Ship of Theseus, rebuilt plank by plank, if enough of you gets swapped out, are you still the same you?
cards.source: Wikipedia: Ship of Theseus; Bomb pulse
cards.more:
The old puzzle asks whether a ship whose every plank has been replaced is still the same ship. Biology adds a twist, because you are not replaced evenly. You may have heard that your whole body renews itself every seven years. It isn't that simple.

In 2005, Kirsty Spalding and colleagues used carbon-14 from Cold War nuclear tests, which got locked into the DNA of cells as they formed, to work out how old human cells are. Many tissues turn over, but the neurons of your cerebral cortex essentially do not; they are about as old as you are. So part of you is constantly renewed, and part has been there all along. Maybe identity lives in the pattern, not the material.

cards.title: Which came first, the chicken or the egg?
cards.text: It's one of the oldest riddles there is, and philosophers argued over it for centuries. But evolution gives a surprisingly clear answer. Before you tap for more, think it through: did the first chicken hatch from an egg, or lay one?
cards.source: Wikipedia: Chicken or the egg
cards.more:
The egg, by a long way. Hard-shelled eggs that could be laid on dry land, the kind reptiles and birds still lay, appeared around 312 million years ago, long before any bird existed. Fish and amphibians laid eggs earlier still.

Even if you only count chicken eggs, the egg wins. Species change gradually, so at some point two birds that were almost chickens produced an egg holding a bird we would call a chicken. The DNA that made it a chicken was already in the egg before anything hatched. There was never a first chicken without parents, just a long line of birds, each very slightly different from the last.

cards.title: Why choice makes us dizzy
cards.text: Kierkegaard compared anxiety to standing at the edge of a cliff. The dizziness isn’t only fear of falling; it’s the awareness that you could jump. For him, anxiety is what freedom feels like from the inside: the vertigo of knowing your life turns on your own choices.
cards.author: Søren Kierkegaard
cards.source: The Concept of Anxiety (1844)
cards.more:
Søren Kierkegaard, a 19th-century Danish thinker often called the first existentialist, published much of his work under made-up names. In The Concept of Anxiety he separates fear, which has an object, from anxiety, which is about possibility itself. Looking down from a height, you feel dizzy partly because nothing is stopping you.

This thread follows that idea through the thinkers who picked it up. Their shared starting point is here: being human means facing choices no rulebook can settle for you. The anxiety isn’t a malfunction. It’s a sign you are taking your freedom seriously. The question the rest of the thread asks is what to do with it.

thread.title: Existentialism in 7 cards

cards.text: If a man knows the wherefore of his existence, then the manner of it can take care of itself.
cards.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
cards.source: Twilight of the Idols, Maxims and Missiles 12 (trans. Anthony M. Ludovici, 1911)
cards.more:
Nietzsche wrote this in 1888 among a run of short, punchy aphorisms. It became famous in the 20th century when the psychiatrist Viktor Frankl, a Holocaust survivor, quoted a version of it in Man’s Search for Meaning to explain how some prisoners found the strength to endure.

For the existentialist story, Nietzsche matters because he argued that the old sources of meaning were fading and people would have to create their own values. If anxiety is the feeling of freedom, a ‘wherefore’ is what gives that freedom a direction. Worth asking yourself: what is my why right now, and does my daily how actually serve it?

thread.title: Existentialism in 7 cards

cards.title: You exist first, then decide what you are
cards.text: A paper knife is designed before it exists: someone decides what it’s for, then makes it. Sartre argued people are the reverse. We exist first, with no built-in purpose, and only then define ourselves through what we do. Nobody is born a coward or a hero. You become one.
cards.author: Jean-Paul Sartre
cards.source: Existentialism Is a Humanism (lecture 1945, published 1946)
cards.more:
Jean-Paul Sartre gave this lecture in Paris in 1945, and it became the best-known summary of existentialism. His slogan was that existence precedes essence. Without a creator who designed human nature in advance, there is no blueprint to consult. We are what we make of ourselves.

That is both thrilling and heavy. It means ‘that’s just how I am’ never fully works as an excuse, because how you are is the sum of your choices so far. Sartre added that in choosing for yourself, you also sketch a picture of what you think a person should be. Every decision is a small vote for a kind of humanity.

thread.title: Existentialism in 7 cards

cards.title: The waiter who plays a waiter
cards.text: Sartre describes a café waiter whose movements are a little too precise and a little too eager, as if he were acting the part. That’s bad faith: pretending you are just a role, a fixed thing, so you don’t have to face your freedom. Its favourite slogan is ‘I had no choice’.
cards.author: Jean-Paul Sartre
cards.source: Being and Nothingness (1943)
cards.more:
If we create ourselves, why do so few people feel free? Sartre’s answer was bad faith, a kind of self-deception in which we hide from our own freedom. The waiter treats ‘waiter’ as his whole essence. The rest of us say things like ‘I’m just not a creative person’ or ‘my job made me do it’.

Sartre isn’t mocking waiters, or roles in general. Roles are fine; the problem is pretending they do the choosing for you. A useful test: notice how often you say ‘I have to’. Some of those are true. Many, looked at honestly, mean ‘I’m choosing to, and I’d rather not own it’.

thread.title: Existentialism in 7 cards

cards.title: My freedom needs yours
cards.text: Simone de Beauvoir pushed existentialism outward. If freedom is what gives life value, she argued, you can’t coherently want it only for yourself. To will yourself free is also to will others free. Treating people as tools betrays the very thing that makes your own choices meaningful.
cards.author: Simone de Beauvoir
cards.source: The Ethics of Ambiguity (1947)
cards.more:
Beauvoir wrote The Ethics of Ambiguity partly to answer a common criticism: if there are no fixed values, isn’t everything permitted? Her reply was no. We are ambiguous creatures, both free and bound by bodies, history and other people, and real freedom only grows in a world where others are free as well.

Two years later, The Second Sex applied this to women, showing how society had cast them as a fixed ‘other’ rather than as free subjects. For this thread, she adds the missing social piece. Owning your freedom also means caring about the conditions that let other people exercise theirs.

thread.title: Existentialism in 7 cards

cards.title: Sisyphus, smiling
cards.text: The gods condemned Sisyphus to push a boulder uphill forever, only for it to roll back down. Camus saw our situation in him: we crave meaning from a universe that stays silent. His answer wasn’t despair but revolt, living fully anyway. He ends by asking us to picture Sisyphus happy.
cards.author: Albert Camus
cards.source: The Myth of Sisyphus (1942)
cards.more:
Camus called the clash between our hunger for meaning and the world’s silence ‘the absurd’. He asked whether it makes life not worth living, and answered no. The absurd isn’t a problem to be solved but a condition to live with, eyes open.

Sisyphus becomes his hero because he knows exactly how hopeless his task is and keeps pushing anyway, owning every step. Camus rejected the existentialist label, but he belongs in this story. Where Sartre says we create meaning, Camus says we can live with intensity even without it. For him, the effort itself can be enough.

thread.title: Existentialism in 7 cards

cards.title: What are you pretending isn’t a choice?
cards.text: Name one thing in your life you describe as ‘just how it is’: a job, a habit, a relationship, a belief about yourself. If you treated it as a choice you keep making every day, what would change?
cards.source: Drawing on Sartre, Being and Nothingness (1943), and Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus (1942)
cards.more:
This question pulls the thread together. Kierkegaard said freedom makes us dizzy. Nietzsche said we need a why. Sartre said there is no fixed human nature, and that we hide from this in bad faith. Beauvoir said real freedom includes other people’s. Camus said we can live fully even when the universe gives no answers.

None of them claimed every circumstance is chosen. Illness, poverty and other people’s actions are real limits. But inside those limits, they argued, there is usually more choice than we admit. Seeing a ‘that’s just how it is’ as a choice doesn’t oblige you to change it. It just makes it yours.

thread.title: Existentialism in 7 cards
