cards.text: …daily to discourse about virtue, and of those other things about which you hear me examining myself and others, is the greatest good of man, and that the unexamined life is not worth living…
cards.author: Socrates (as written by Plato)
cards.source: Apology, 38a (trans. Benjamin Jowett, 1871)
cards.more:
Socrates said this at his trial in Athens in 399 BC, after the jury had found him guilty of impiety and corrupting the young. Instead of begging for mercy, he explained that he could not stop questioning people, because examining how to live is the most valuable thing a person can do.

‘Examined’ here means tested in conversation: asking what you believe about justice, courage or the good life, and whether those beliefs hold up. The jury sentenced him to death. Nearly 2,500 years later, the line is still philosophy’s mission statement. A small version for today: pick one thing you’re sure of, and ask yourself why.

cards.text: …men come to be builders, for instance, by building; harp-players, by playing on the harp: exactly so, by doing just actions we come to be just; by doing the actions of self-mastery we come to be perfected in self-mastery; and by doing brave actions brave.
cards.author: Aristotle
cards.source: Nicomachean Ethics, Book 2.1 (trans. D. P. Chase)
cards.more:
Aristotle’s point is that character is learned like a craft. Nobody becomes a harpist by reading about harps, and nobody becomes brave or fair by admiring bravery or fairness. You become what you repeatedly do.

This was a quietly radical idea. It means virtue isn’t a gift you either have or lack; it’s a skill built through practice, clumsy at first, until it becomes second nature. If you want to be more patient, generous or honest, don’t wait until you feel like that kind of person. Act like one, again and again, and the feeling tends to follow. Your habits are slowly writing your character.

cards.text: …all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber.
cards.author: Blaise Pascal
cards.source: Pensées, 139 (trans. W. F. Trotter)
cards.more:
Blaise Pascal was a mathematician and inventor who, in his last years, gathered notes for a defence of Christianity. He died in 1662 before finishing it, and the fragments were published as the Pensées, or ‘thoughts’. This one comes from a section on diversion.

Pascal noticed that people chase games, wars and busyness largely to avoid sitting alone with their thoughts, especially thoughts about their own condition and mortality. In a 2014 study, many participants chose to give themselves a mild electric shock rather than sit alone with nothing to do for a few minutes. Try ten minutes with no phone, and notice what you reach for.

cards.text: When I play with my cat who knows whether I do not make her more sport than she makes me? We mutually divert one another with our play.
cards.author: Michel de Montaigne
cards.source: Essays, Book 2.12, Apology for Raimond Sebond (trans. Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt)
cards.more:
Michel de Montaigne more or less invented the essay, a word that means ‘attempt’ in French. This line sits inside his longest essay, where he pokes holes in human arrogance. We assume animals are dim, but on what evidence? We can’t see inside them any more than they can see inside us.

The cat question is playful, but the point is serious. Much of what we feel certain about is just the view from our own side. Montaigne’s motto was ‘What do I know?’ Next time you are sure what someone else is thinking, or why they are doing something, try his trick and picture the scene from their side.

cards.text: Two things fill the mind with ever new and increasing admiration and awe, the oftener and the more steadily we reflect on them: the starry heavens above and the moral law within.
cards.author: Immanuel Kant
cards.source: Critique of Practical Reason, Conclusion (trans. Thomas Kingsmill Abbott)
cards.more:
This is how Kant opens the conclusion of the Critique of Practical Reason, his 1788 book on ethics. It’s one of the few lyrical moments from a famously dense writer, and probably his most quoted sentence.

The two wonders mirror each other. The night sky shows how tiny we are: one creature on a speck in a vast universe. The moral law shows how large we are: beings who can recognise duty and act on reason rather than impulse. Kant located human dignity in that second fact. Next clear night, look up for a minute, then ask what you owe the people around you.

cards.text: Philosophy is to be studied, not for the sake of any definite answers to its questions, since no definite answers can, as a rule, be known to be true, but rather for the sake of the questions themselves…
cards.author: Bertrand Russell
cards.source: The Problems of Philosophy, Chapter 15: The Value of Philosophy (1912)
cards.more:
Bertrand Russell wrote The Problems of Philosophy in 1912 as a short introduction for general readers, and this comes from its final chapter. He admits that philosophy rarely produces settled answers, partly because once a question can be answered definitely, it tends to become its own science.

So what’s the point? Russell says the questions widen your sense of what is possible and loosen the grip of prejudices you never chose. Someone who never asks them lives inside the beliefs of their time and place without noticing. Philosophy’s gift, in his view, isn’t certainty but a larger, freer mind. The questions are the reward.

cards.text: When we read, another person thinks for us: we merely repeat his mental process.
cards.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
cards.source: On Reading and Books, in Essays of Schopenhauer (trans. Mrs. Rudolf Dircks)
cards.more:
Arthur Schopenhauer, the 19th-century German philosopher best known for his pessimism, was also sharp about reading. The essay goes on to argue that someone who reads all day, without pausing to think, gradually loses the ability to think for himself, just as a man who is always riding forgets how to walk.

It’s a pointed warning to find in a feed of quotes like this one. Reading gives you raw material; thinking is what turns it into your own understanding. A simple habit: after reading anything worth keeping, close it and write two sentences about what you think, not what it said.

cards.text: …all things excellent are as difficult as they are rare.
cards.author: Baruch Spinoza
cards.source: Ethics, Part 5, Proposition 42, Note (trans. R. H. M. Elwes, 1883)
cards.more:
These are the last words of Spinoza’s Ethics, a book laid out like geometry, with definitions, axioms and proofs. Spinoza argued that freedom comes from understanding: the more clearly we see the causes of our emotions, the less they push us around.

In this closing note he admits the path is very hard and few take it. It’s an honest ending, and a reassuring one. If something worthwhile feels difficult, that isn’t proof you’re doing it wrong. Spinoza lived modestly, supporting himself partly by grinding lenses, and turned down a professorship at Heidelberg, perhaps to protect his freedom to think.

cards.title: The banality of evil
cards.text: Reporting on the trial of Nazi official Adolf Eichmann, Hannah Arendt expected a monster. She found a careerist who spoke in clichés and seemed never to have really thought about what he was doing. Her unsettling conclusion: enormous evil can come from ordinary people who stop thinking.
cards.author: Hannah Arendt
cards.source: Eichmann in Jerusalem: A Report on the Banality of Evil (1963)
cards.more:
Arendt travelled to Jerusalem in 1961 to cover the trial for The New Yorker, and her book caused an uproar. Critics accused her of excusing Eichmann. She wasn’t. Her point was that he was frighteningly normal: ambitious, obedient and thoughtless rather than demonic.

The idea shifts where we look for danger. If evil required monsters, most of us could relax. If it can come from people following orders, chasing promotions and never asking what their work actually does, then the safeguard is ordinary thinking. Stop now and then and ask: what am I really taking part in?

cards.title: Socrates never wrote a word
cards.text: Socrates, perhaps the most famous philosopher in the Western tradition, wrote nothing at all. Nearly everything we know about him comes from accounts written after his death, mostly by his students Plato and Xenophon, usually in the form of dialogues.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Socrates
cards.more:
This creates what scholars call the Socratic problem: how much of ‘Socrates’ is the real man, and how much is Plato putting his own ideas in his teacher’s mouth? Plato’s Socrates and Xenophon’s don’t always sound alike, and the comic playwright Aristophanes mocked yet another version on stage.

In Plato’s Phaedrus, Socrates even voices a suspicion of writing: a text can’t answer back when you question it, and it can give the appearance of wisdom without the substance. Whatever his reasons, his method lived on through conversation. A good reminder that some of the best thinking happens out loud, with someone pushing back.

cards.title: The philosopher who lived in a jar
cards.text: Diogenes the Cynic lived in Athens with almost nothing, sheltering in a large ceramic storage jar. He also wandered public places in daylight carrying a lit lamp, saying he was looking for a human being.
cards.author: Diogenes of Sinope
cards.source: Wikipedia: Diogenes
cards.more:
Diogenes, who lived in the 4th century BC, treated his whole life as a philosophical performance. If the good life means living according to nature, he reasoned, most of what society prizes, like wealth, manners and status, is clutter. Later Roman writers turned his jar into a barrel, which is how he’s usually pictured today.

The most famous story has Alexander the Great visiting him and asking if there was anything he wanted. Diogenes answered that Alexander could stand a little out of his sun. Whether or not every story is true, he leaves a sharp question: how much of what you own and do is actually needed?

cards.title: Descartes and the 5 a.m. lessons
cards.text: René Descartes, the philosopher of ‘I think, therefore I am’, agreed in 1649 to tutor Queen Christina of Sweden three times a week at 5 a.m. in her cold, draughty castle. He caught pneumonia and died in Stockholm in February 1650.
cards.author: René Descartes
cards.source: Wikipedia: René Descartes
cards.more:
By 1649 Descartes was one of the most famous thinkers in Europe, and Christina invited him to her court to set up a scientific academy and teach her his ideas. The arrangement went badly. She rejected his mechanical philosophy, and he didn’t share her passion for ancient Greek. By mid-January they had met only four or five times.

Pneumonia is the standard account of his death, though other causes have been suggested over the years, including poisoning theories linked to the religious tensions of the day. Either way, it’s a sad end for a man whose Discourse on the Method describes his breakthrough coming during a winter spent alone with his thoughts, undisturbed.

cards.title: The ring of invisibility
cards.text: Imagine a ring that makes you invisible whenever you like, so no one would ever know what you did. Would you still behave exactly as you do now? If not, what is your honesty actually resting on?
cards.author: Plato
cards.source: Republic, Book 2 (trans. Benjamin Jowett)
cards.more:
In Plato’s Republic, Glaucon tells the story of Gyges, a shepherd who finds a ring of invisibility and uses it to seduce a queen, kill a king and seize the throne. His challenge to Socrates: people are only just because they fear getting caught. Give anyone the ring and they would act the same way.

Much of the rest of the Republic is Socrates’ long answer: that justice is good for the soul in itself, a kind of inner harmony, not just protection against punishment. The question is worth answering honestly. The gap between how you act when watched and when unseen is a decent measure of character.

cards.title: The first guess at atoms
cards.text: Around 400 BC, Democritus reasoned that if you keep cutting matter in half, you must eventually reach pieces that cannot be cut. He called them atoms, meaning uncuttable, and claimed that everything around us is just atoms moving through empty space.
cards.author: Democritus
cards.source: Known through later ancient writers (c. 5th to 4th century BC); Wikipedia: Democritus
cards.more:
Democritus lived roughly from 460 to 370 BC and built on ideas from the earlier thinker Leucippus. None of his own books survive; we know his views through later writers who quoted or argued with him.

He had no way to test any of this. It was pure reasoning: matter can't be divisible forever, so there must be a smallest piece, too small for the senses to detect. For about two thousand years the idea stayed there, admired by some and dismissed by many.

This thread follows how a philosopher's hunch became one of the best-tested facts in science, and what it took to find real evidence.

thread.title: How do we know atoms are real? (7 cards)

cards.title: Chemistry counts in whole numbers
cards.text: In the early 1800s, John Dalton saw that elements combine in simple whole-number ratios. Carbon and oxygen form two different gases, and for the same amount of carbon, one contains exactly twice as much oxygen as the other. Never 1.37 times. Always whole steps.
cards.source: Dalton, A New System of Chemical Philosophy (1808); Wikipedia: John Dalton, Law of multiple proportions
cards.more:
The two gases are carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide. Dalton's explanation was simple: each element is made of identical atoms with a characteristic weight, and compounds form when whole atoms join. You can't add half an atom, so the ratios jump in whole numbers. His New System of Chemical Philosophy (1808) laid this out with the first table of relative atomic weights.

It was a huge step, but many scientists stayed cautious. Atoms were a handy bookkeeping device, they said, not necessarily real objects. Nobody had seen one. The decisive evidence would come from an unexpected place: a botanist's microscope.

thread.title: How do we know atoms are real? (7 cards)

cards.title: The jiggle that would not stop
cards.text: In 1827, botanist Robert Brown watched tiny particles from pollen grains suspended in water. They jittered and zigzagged nonstop, for no visible reason. He repeated it with specks of glass and rock dust, and those jiggled too. So it wasn't life. Something invisible was shoving them.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Brownian motion
cards.more:
Brown was careful. A natural first guess was that the motion came from some vital force in the pollen, so he tested particles of inorganic matter. They danced in exactly the same way, which ruled out biology.

For decades the motion stayed a curiosity. People suspected heat currents, vibrations or evaporation, but the jiggling carried on no matter how still things were kept, and it never ran down. The real explanation, when it finally arrived in 1905, turned this odd observation into the first direct window onto the molecular world, and settled an argument that had lasted since Democritus.

thread.title: How do we know atoms are real? (7 cards)

cards.title: Fingerprints of invisible molecules
cards.text: In 1905 Einstein showed that Brownian motion is exactly what you'd expect if water were made of countless molecules randomly battering each particle, and he predicted how far a particle should drift over time. In 1908 Jean Perrin measured it. The numbers matched. Atoms had left fingerprints.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Brownian motion; Nobel Prize in Physics 1926
cards.more:
Einstein's insight was statistical. One molecule is far too small to budge a visible particle, but enormous numbers of them hitting from all sides, slightly unevenly from moment to moment, add up to a random walk. His formula tied the size of that wandering to how many molecules a given amount of substance contains.

Perrin's painstaking experiments with tiny suspended grains confirmed the prediction, and most remaining sceptics were won over. Perrin received the 1926 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on the discontinuous structure of matter. Atoms had gone from a useful hypothesis to something measured.

thread.title: How do we know atoms are real? (7 cards)

cards.title: Atoms are almost entirely empty
cards.text: In 1909, Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden fired alpha particles at thin metal foil. Most passed straight through, but about 1 in 8,000 bounced back. Rutherford later compared it to an artillery shell rebounding off tissue paper. The explanation: nearly all of an atom's mass sits in a tiny nucleus.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Rutherford scattering experiments; Atomic nucleus
cards.more:
Rutherford worked out what this meant in 1911. If an atom's positive charge and mass were spread out evenly, as the leading model assumed, nothing should ever bounce backward. Only a tiny, dense, positively charged core could fling a fast alpha particle back toward its source.

That core, the nucleus, is astonishingly small. Depending on the element, an atom is roughly 27,000 to 60,000 times wider than its nucleus. If a nucleus were the size of a pea, its atom would be a few hundred metres across. Everything you touch is mostly empty space, which raises an obvious question.

thread.title: How do we know atoms are real? (7 cards)

cards.title: Why can't you walk through walls?
cards.text: If atoms are almost entirely empty space, then your hand and a table are mostly nothing. So why does your hand stop when it meets the table, instead of drifting through it like two clouds of gnats passing each other?
cards.source: Wikipedia: Pauli exclusion principle
cards.more:
Two things stop you. First, the outer parts of atoms are clouds of negatively charged electrons, and when two atoms get close, those clouds repel each other electrically. What you feel as touch is that repulsion, not solid lumps meeting.

Second, and deeper, is the Pauli exclusion principle, formulated by Wolfgang Pauli in 1925: no two electrons can occupy the same quantum state. Electrons can't all pile into the same space, so atoms resist being squeezed together. In the late 1960s, Freeman Dyson and Andrew Lenard proved that this rule is why ordinary matter is stable and takes up room at all. Emptiness, it turns out, can be very firm.

thread.title: How do we know atoms are real? (7 cards)

cards.title: The one sentence worth saving
cards.text: Richard Feynman asked: if a catastrophe wiped out all scientific knowledge and only one sentence could be passed on, which would carry the most information? His pick was the atomic hypothesis. Everything is built from atoms, tiny bits forever in motion that pull on each other when close and push back when pressed together.
cards.author: Richard Feynman
cards.source: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. I, ch. 1, Atoms in Motion (1963)
cards.more:
Feynman's point was that this one idea unlocks an enormous amount, given a little imagination: why water evaporates, what temperature really is, why solids hold their shape and gases spread out.

It also ties this thread together. The idea began as Democritus's pure guess, became Dalton's bookkeeping for chemistry, showed itself in Brown's jiggling particles, was measured by Einstein and Perrin, and was cracked open by Rutherford to reveal a mostly empty interior held firm by quantum rules. Each step needed the one before it. That's how science usually works: not a single flash of genius, but a long relay in which every runner tests what the last one handed over.

thread.title: How do we know atoms are real? (7 cards)

cards.text: There is not a law under which any part of this universe is governed which does not come into play, and is touched upon in these phenomena. There is no better, there is no more open door by which you can enter into the study of natural philosophy, than by considering the physical phenomena of a candle.
cards.author: Michael Faraday
cards.source: The Chemical History of a Candle, Lecture I (1861)
cards.more:
Faraday gave these talks as a course of six lectures for a young audience at the Royal Institution in London, and they were published in 1861. Using little more than candles, he showed how the wax melts into a cup, climbs the wick, turns to vapour and burns, and how burning produces water and carbon dioxide.

His larger point still holds. You don't need exotic equipment to meet the laws of nature; gravity, heat, chemistry and light are all at work in one small flame. Faraday himself had little formal schooling and began as a bookbinder's apprentice, which may be why he believed so firmly that anyone could learn to look at the world this way.

cards.text: Science is built up with facts, as a house is with stones. But a collection of facts is no more a science than a heap of stones is a house.
cards.author: Henri Poincaré
cards.source: Science and Hypothesis, ch. 9, in The Foundations of Science (Halsted trans., 1913)
cards.more:
Henri Poincaré was one of the great mathematicians and physicists of his era, and he thought hard about what scientists are actually doing. His point here is that data alone explains nothing. A pile of measurements becomes science only when someone finds the pattern that ties them together.

Right after this line he adds that, above all, the scientist must foresee. A good theory is like a well-built house: you can walk into rooms no one has entered yet and trust the floor to hold. Gathering facts is necessary, but the real work is organising them into something that predicts what you haven't measured.

cards.text: To doubt everything and to believe everything are two equally convenient solutions; each saves us from thinking.
cards.author: Henri Poincaré
cards.source: Science and Hypothesis, Introduction, in The Foundations of Science (Halsted trans., 1913)
cards.more:
Poincaré wrote this in the introduction to Science and Hypothesis, first published in French in 1902. He was pushing back against two lazy attitudes toward science: treating every claim as settled truth, or dismissing the whole enterprise as arbitrary guesswork.

His alternative was harder. He wanted readers to examine each hypothesis on its own terms, asking which are necessary, which are convenient conventions, and which can be checked by experiment. That habit of sorting, rather than swallowing or rejecting everything wholesale, is still one of the best defences against both gullibility and cynicism.

cards.text: The scientist does not study nature because it is useful; he studies it because he delights in it, and he delights in it because it is beautiful. If nature were not beautiful, it would not be worth knowing, and if nature were not worth knowing, life would not be worth living.
cards.author: Henri Poincaré
cards.source: Science and Method, Book I, ch. 1, in The Foundations of Science (Halsted trans., 1913)
cards.more:
Science and Method appeared in French in 1908. In this chapter, titled The Choice of Facts, Poincaré asks how scientists decide what is worth studying when there are endless facts available. His answer is surprising from a hard-headed mathematician: they are guided by a sense of beauty.

He immediately clarifies that he doesn't mean colours or surface appearances. He means a deeper beauty, the harmonious order of the parts, which a pure intelligence can grasp. Simple laws that unite many facts tend to be both beautiful and useful, which is exactly why chasing that kind of beauty has served science so well.

cards.text: Science is, I believe, nothing but trained and organized common sense, differing from the latter only as a veteran may differ from a raw recruit
cards.author: Thomas Henry Huxley
cards.source: On the Educational Value of the Natural History Sciences (1854), in Lay Sermons, Addresses and Reviews (1870)
cards.more:
Thomas Henry Huxley, the biologist later famous as Darwin's fiercest public defender, gave this address in 1854 to argue that science deserved a place in ordinary education. Science, he said, was not a mysterious priesthood. It uses the same reasoning everyone uses daily, just sharpened by practice and checked more carefully.

That's a hopeful thought. The habits behind good science, like noticing, comparing, testing a guess and changing your mind when the evidence says so, are available to anyone. What separates the veteran from the recruit is training, not a different kind of brain.

cards.title: Measuring the Earth with shadows
cards.text: In the 3rd century BC, Eratosthenes learned that at noon on the summer solstice, the Sun shone straight down into a well at Syene, while rods in Alexandria still cast shadows. The shadow angle was about 7.2 degrees, one fiftieth of a circle. So Earth's circumference was fifty times the distance between the cities.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Eratosthenes
cards.more:
The logic is lovely. The Sun is so far away that its rays arrive essentially parallel. On a flat Earth, rods in both cities would cast identical shadows. The difference in angle tells you how much the surface curves between them.

Eratosthenes put the answer at around 250,000 stadia. Nobody is sure exactly how long his stadion was, so historians still argue about his precision, but by many estimates he came impressively close to the true figure of about 40,000 kilometres. His own book on the method is lost; we know it through a simplified retelling by the later writer Cleomedes. All it took was a shadow, a distance and geometry.

cards.title: Found on the Sun before Earth
cards.text: Helium was detected on the Sun before anyone found it on Earth. During a solar eclipse in 1868, astronomers saw a yellow line in sunlight that matched no known element. Norman Lockyer proposed a new one and named it after the Greek word for Sun. It was isolated on Earth in 1895.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Helium
cards.more:
Every element emits and absorbs light at its own set of colours, like a barcode. Spread sunlight into a spectrum and those barcodes appear as sharp lines. The new yellow line sat close to two known lines of sodium, and at first it was assumed to be sodium.

Lockyer's bold guess went unconfirmed for 27 years, until William Ramsay found helium in gas released from a uranium mineral. Rare as it is on Earth, helium is the second most abundant element in the universe, after hydrogen, and most of it was made in the Big Bang. We just had to look up to find it first.

cards.title: Two Nobels in two sciences
cards.text: Marie Curie won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903 and the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1911. She remains the only person ever to win Nobel Prizes in two different scientific fields. She was also the first woman to win a Nobel Prize at all.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Marie Curie
cards.more:
The 1903 physics prize, shared with her husband Pierre and with Henri Becquerel, recognised research on radioactivity, a term Marie Curie coined. The 1911 chemistry prize was hers alone, for discovering the elements polonium and radium. She named polonium after her native Poland.

The Curies had no proper laboratory and did much of their work in a converted shed, handling radioactive material long before its dangers were understood. Her papers are still radioactive and are kept in lead-lined boxes; visitors who consult them wear protective clothing. She died in 1934 of aplastic anaemia, very likely caused by her years of radiation exposure.

cards.title: A metal that melts in your hand
cards.text: Gallium is a soft, silvery metal that melts at about 29.76 °C, cooler than your body. Hold a piece in your palm and it slowly slumps into a shiny puddle. Leave it in a cool room and it turns solid again.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Gallium
cards.more:
Gallium is one of only four metals that are liquid at or near room temperature, alongside mercury, caesium and rubidium. It also starred in a great moment for chemistry. In 1871, Dmitri Mendeleev predicted an undiscovered element he called eka-aluminium, leaving a gap for it in his periodic table and forecasting its properties.

When Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran discovered gallium in 1875, it fit. Mendeleev had predicted a density of about 5.9 grams per cubic centimetre; the measured value is 5.904. Successes like this convinced chemists that the periodic table wasn't just a tidy chart but a real map of how elements behave.

cards.title: Old windows are not melting
cards.text: You may have heard that old church windows are thicker at the bottom because glass is a slowly flowing liquid. It isn't true. The panes were uneven from the day they were made. One study estimated medieval glass flows at most about a nanometre in a billion years.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Glass (Reputed flow)
cards.more:
Older methods of making flat glass produced sheets with ripples and uneven thickness. The near-perfect float glass we use today only became widespread in the 1960s. So the lumps and sags in old windows were there from the start.

Glass is an amorphous solid: its atoms are jumbled like a liquid's, but locked in place like a solid's. A 2017 study looked at glass from Westminster Abbey dating to 1268 and calculated how fast it could possibly flow at room temperature. Even across the entire age of the universe, the change would be far too small to see.

cards.title: Why ice floats
cards.text: Most substances shrink when they freeze. Water does the opposite: it expands by about 9 percent, so ice floats. That is why lakes freeze from the top down, leaving liquid water underneath where fish can survive the winter.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Ice
cards.more:
The reason is hydrogen bonding. In liquid water, molecules tumble past each other and pack fairly closely. As water freezes, each molecule locks into a hexagonal lattice held at fixed angles, and that open structure takes up more room. Ice at ordinary pressure has a density of about 0.917 grams per cubic centimetre, against roughly 1 for liquid water.

The consequences are huge. Floating ice insulates the water below, so lakes rarely freeze solid. Water that freezes in cracks pries rocks apart, slowly turning mountains into soil. And it's why a forgotten bottle in the freezer can burst. Water isn't entirely alone in this; gallium also expands when it solidifies.

cards.title: Good theories stick their necks out
cards.text: Karl Popper argued that what makes a theory scientific isn't that evidence supports it, since almost any idea can find supporters. It's that the theory forbids something: it makes a risky prediction that could turn out wrong. A claim no possible observation could ever refute isn't strong. It just isn't science.
cards.author: Karl Popper
cards.source: The Logic of Scientific Discovery (1934)
cards.more:
Popper was struck by a contrast. Einstein's general relativity predicted exactly how much starlight should bend passing the Sun, and the 1919 eclipse observations could have proved it wrong. Meanwhile, some fashionable theories of his day seemed able to explain any outcome at all, which Popper saw as a weakness dressed up as strength.

Philosophers still debate his criterion, called falsifiability, and real science is messier than any single rule. But as a working test it's powerful. When someone offers you an idea, ask: what result would show this is wrong? If the answer is nothing, be careful.

cards.title: Can a demon beat the laws of heat?
cards.text: Imagine a tiny being guarding a door between two boxes of gas. It lets only fast molecules through one way and slow ones the other. Without pushing anything, it makes one side hot and the other cold, apparently beating the law that heat flows from hot to cold. What's the catch?
cards.source: Wikipedia: Maxwell's demon
cards.more:
James Clerk Maxwell proposed this puzzle in 1867 to show that the second law of thermodynamics is statistical rather than absolute. It nagged physicists for a century.

The resolution involves information. To sort molecules, the demon must measure them and remember the results. In 1929 Leo Szilard linked measurement to entropy, and later work by Rolf Landauer and Charles Bennett showed that the unavoidable cost lies in erasing the demon's memory to make room for new measurements. Erasing information always gives off heat, enough to cancel out what the sorting gains. The second law survives, and we learned something remarkable along the way: information is physical.

cards.title: You see the Sun as it was
cards.text: Sunlight takes about 8.3 minutes to reach Earth. So the Sun you see in the sky is the Sun as it was eight minutes ago. Light is the fastest thing there is, and even it needs time to cross space. That delay is also the best ruler we have.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Sunlight; Speed of light
cards.more:
Light travels at exactly 299,792,458 metres per second in a vacuum; the metre is now defined by it. That's fast enough to circle Earth about seven and a half times in one second. But the Sun is around 150 million kilometres away, so the trip still takes over eight minutes.

This turns time into a measuring tape. The Moon is about 1.3 light-seconds away, the Sun about 8.3 light-minutes. The farther out we look, the further back in time we see. This thread climbs the cosmic distance ladder one rung at a time, from our own star to the edge of everything we can observe.

thread.title: How big is the universe? (7 cards)

cards.title: The first distance to a star
cards.text: In 1838, Friedrich Bessel became the first person to measure the distance to a star other than the Sun. He watched 61 Cygni shift very slightly as Earth circled the Sun, and calculated it was about 10.4 light-years away. The modern value is about 11.4.
cards.source: Wikipedia: 61 Cygni; Stellar parallax
cards.more:
The method is parallax. Hold up a finger and look at it with one eye, then the other: it jumps against the background. As Earth swings from one side of its orbit to the other, nearby stars shift against more distant ones in the same way. Measure the shift, and geometry gives the distance.

The catch is that the shift is tiny. For 61 Cygni it's under a third of an arcsecond, smaller than a coin seen from 10 kilometres away. Astronomers hunted for stellar parallax for centuries. For most of the 20th century, though, parallax could only reach out a few hundred light-years, so a new ruler was needed.

thread.title: How big is the universe? (7 cards)

cards.title: A light-year is a distance
cards.text: A light-year is how far light travels in a year: about 9.46 trillion kilometres. The nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.25 light-years away. At the speed of Voyager 1, one of our fastest spacecraft, the trip would take about 75,000 years.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Light-year; Proxima Centauri; Voyager 1
cards.more:
Voyager 1 is travelling at roughly 61,000 kilometres per hour, and it still needs tens of thousands of years to cover a distance light crosses in just over four. That gap is why every star in the night sky is, for now, completely out of reach.

Light-years carry a hidden lesson too. When you look at Proxima Centauri, you see light that left it more than four years ago. And our galaxy, the Milky Way, is close to 90,000 light-years across, holding somewhere between 100 and 400 billion stars. Parallax mapped our neighbourhood. To measure the galaxy and what lies beyond it, astronomers needed a star whose true brightness they could know in advance.

thread.title: How big is the universe? (7 cards)

cards.title: Stars that reveal their own brightness
cards.text: Henrietta Swan Leavitt, measuring stars on photographic plates at Harvard, noticed in 1908 that certain pulsing stars, Cepheids, follow a rule: the slower they pulse, the brighter they truly are. By 1912 she had pinned the relationship down. Astronomers suddenly had a yardstick for the cosmos.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Henrietta Swan Leavitt
cards.more:
Leavitt was one of the women Harvard College Observatory employed as human computers, cataloguing the positions and brightness of stars from glass plates. She was paid 30 cents an hour. Studying Cepheids in the Small Magellanic Cloud, she realised that since they were all at roughly the same distance from us, differences in how bright they looked reflected real differences in power.

That made Cepheids standard candles. Time a Cepheid's pulse and you know how bright it really is; compare that with how bright it appears, and you know how far away it is. Leavitt died in 1921, before her yardstick was used for one of the most dramatic measurements in astronomy.

thread.title: How big is the universe? (7 cards)

cards.title: The day the universe got bigger
cards.text: In the early 1920s, astronomers still argued over whether the Milky Way was the whole universe. Then Edwin Hubble found Cepheid stars in the Andromeda Nebula, applied Leavitt's rule, and showed it lay far outside our galaxy. Andromeda is a galaxy of its own, about 2.5 million light-years away.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Andromeda Galaxy
cards.more:
In 1920, Harlow Shapley and Heber Curtis held the Great Debate over whether spiral nebulae were clouds inside our galaxy or separate island universes. Hubble settled it in 1925, using photographs from the 100-inch Hooker telescope at Mount Wilson.

Almost overnight, the universe went from one galaxy to an uncountable number of them. And the light-travel lesson still applies: the faint glow of Andromeda that reaches your eyes on a dark night left it about 2.5 million years ago, long before our own species existed. Next comes the strangest rung of the ladder.

thread.title: How big is the universe? (7 cards)

cards.title: Seeing farther than light could travel?
cards.text: The universe is about 13.8 billion years old, so no light can have travelled for longer than that. Yet the edge of the observable universe is about 46.5 billion light-years away. How can we see things farther away than light could travel in the entire age of the universe?
cards.source: Wikipedia: Observable universe
cards.more:
The answer is that space itself has been expanding the whole time. In the late 1920s, astronomers including Hubble found that distant galaxies are moving away from us, and the farther they are, the faster they recede. Light from the most distant regions set out when those regions were much closer. While it travelled, the space it crossed kept stretching.

So 46.5 billion light-years is roughly where those sources are now, not where they were when the light left. The light arrives stretched to longer, redder wavelengths, which is how we measure the expansion. Beyond the observable edge, the universe very likely continues. We just can't receive light from it.

thread.title: How big is the universe? (7 cards)

cards.title: Home, from six billion kilometres
cards.text: In 1990, partly at Carl Sagan's urging, Voyager 1 turned its camera back toward home from over 6 billion kilometres away. Earth showed up as a speck smaller than one pixel. Sagan argued that this tiny dot is the clearest reminder that all our history and quarrels happen on one small, fragile world.
cards.author: Carl Sagan
cards.source: Pale Blue Dot (1994); Wikipedia: Pale Blue Dot
cards.more:
The photo was taken on February 14, 1990, as part of a Family Portrait of the solar system. Soon afterwards, Voyager 1's cameras were switched off for good to save power. Earth takes up about 0.12 of a pixel, caught in a streak of scattered sunlight.

It's the right place to end this thread. We started with light taking eight minutes to arrive from the Sun, then climbed through parallax, light-years, Leavitt's pulsing stars and Hubble's galaxies to the edge of the observable universe. Sagan's point was that this sense of scale isn't just trivia to memorise. It can change how we see ourselves, and how gently we treat each other.

thread.title: How big is the universe? (7 cards)

cards.text: I feel sure that the surface of the Moon is not perfectly smooth, free from inequalities and exactly spherical, as a large school of philosophers considers with regard to the Moon and the other heavenly bodies, but that, on the contrary, it is full of inequalities, uneven, full of hollows and protuberances, just like the surface of the Earth itself
cards.author: Galileo Galilei
cards.source: The Sidereal Messenger (1610), trans. Edward Stafford Carlos (1880)
cards.more:
Galileo didn't invent the telescope, but he built improved versions and, crucially, pointed them at the sky. Through an instrument that made the Moon look about thirty times wider, he watched the line between light and dark. Bright points appeared inside the shadowed part, then grew and joined the lit region: mountain peaks catching the sunrise.

That mattered because the old view held that heavenly bodies were perfect spheres, made of a different substance from our messy Earth. A Moon with mountains and valleys was a world, not an ornament. Sidereus Nuncius was published on March 13, 1610, and it was the first scientific work based on observations through a telescope.

cards.text: the Galaxy is nothing else but a mass of innumerable stars planted together in clusters. Upon whatever part of it you direct the telescope straightway a vast crowd of stars presents itself to view
cards.author: Galileo Galilei
cards.source: The Sidereal Messenger (1610), trans. Edward Stafford Carlos (1880)
cards.more:
For all of human history, the Milky Way had been a soft band of light across the night sky, and philosophers argued about what it might be. Galileo's small telescope settled it in an instant: the glow was the combined light of stars too faint and too crowded for the naked eye to separate.

It was a first hint of how enormous the universe might be. If a faint smudge could hold countless suns, what else lay beyond the reach of our eyes? It took three more centuries to learn that the Milky Way is a vast disc-shaped galaxy, that we live inside it, and that it is only one galaxy among a great many.

cards.text: This whole earth which we inhabit is but a point in space. How far apart, think you, dwell the two most distant inhabitants of yonder star, the breadth of whose disk cannot be appreciated by our instruments? Why should I feel lonely? is not our planet in the Milky Way?
cards.author: Henry David Thoreau
cards.source: Walden, ch. 5, Solitude (1854)
cards.more:
Thoreau lived alone in a small cabin by Walden Pond in Massachusetts from 1845 to 1847, and people kept asking whether he got lonely out there, especially on rainy and snowy nights. This was his reply.

His argument is a quietly cosmic one. Measured against the distances between stars, the distance between his cabin and the town is nothing. Loneliness, he goes on to say, isn't measured in miles at all. It's an odd and lovely comfort: you are never far from anyone, because all of us are riding the same speck of rock through the same galaxy.

cards.text: A Man that is of Copernicus's Opinion, that this Earth of ours is a Planet, carry'd round and enlighten'd by the Sun, like the rest of the Planets, cannot but sometimes think, that it's not improbable that the rest of the Planets have their Dress and Furniture, and perhaps their Inhabitants too as well as this Earth of ours
cards.author: Christiaan Huygens
cards.source: The Celestial Worlds Discover'd, Book I (English trans., 1698)
cards.more:
Christiaan Huygens was one of the sharpest scientists of the 1600s. Grinding his own telescope lenses, he discovered Saturn's largest moon, Titan, and was the first to explain Saturn's odd appearance as a thin, flat ring. Shortly before his death in 1695 he finished this book, known in Latin as Cosmotheoros, and arranged for it to be published only after he died.

His reasoning is a direct consequence of the Copernican revolution. If Earth is just one planet among several, why should it be the only one with life? Huygens had no way to check. More than three centuries later, with thousands of planets found around other stars, we are still asking his question.

cards.text: one can not resist the temptation to utter a vigorous protest, and to declare that this glorious science is not the grinning mathematical skeleton that it has been represented to be.
cards.author: Garrett P. Serviss
cards.source: Astronomy with an Opera-glass, Introduction (1888)
cards.more:
Serviss was an American journalist who wanted ordinary people to fall in love with the sky. For this book he surveyed the constellations visible from New York using only an opera glass, and promised readers he described nothing he hadn't seen himself.

He opens with a funny story. When Venus blazed in the evening sky in 1887, some New Yorkers decided it must be an electric balloon sent up every night by Thomas Edison. His cure for that kind of confusion was simple: you don't need an observatory to know the sky. A pair of binoculars and a few clear evenings will show you lunar craters, Jupiter's moons and star clusters the naked eye can't separate.

cards.title: A teaspoon heavier than mountains
cards.text: A neutron star packs about 1.4 times the Sun's mass into a ball roughly 20 kilometres across. Its material is so dense that one teaspoon would have a mass of over 5.5 trillion kilograms, around 900 times the mass of the Great Pyramid of Giza.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Neutron star
cards.more:
Neutron stars are what remain after some massive stars explode as supernovae. The core collapses under its own gravity so violently that its matter is crushed into a ball made mostly of neutrons, packed as tightly as the particles inside an atomic nucleus.

They are extreme in every way. As the core collapses it spins up, so newborn neutron stars can rotate several hundred times per second. Some sweep beams of radiation past Earth like lighthouses and are seen as pulsars, first discovered by Jocelyn Bell Burnell and Antony Hewish in 1967. When two neutron stars merge, they can forge heavy elements, including gold.

cards.title: A day longer than a year
cards.text: Venus takes about 243 Earth days to spin once on its axis, but only about 225 days to orbit the Sun. One rotation lasts longer than its whole year. It also spins backwards compared with most planets, so on Venus the Sun rises in the west.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Venus
cards.more:
Because Venus spins slowly backwards while also moving around the Sun, the time from one sunrise to the next works out to about 117 Earth days. So a Venusian solar day is shorter than its rotation, but still very long.

You wouldn't enjoy the view. Venus is wrapped in a thick carbon dioxide atmosphere that traps heat in a runaway greenhouse effect, keeping the surface at around 464 °C. That makes it hotter than Mercury, even though Venus is nearly twice as far from the Sun. It's a planet almost the size of Earth that shows how differently two worlds can turn out.

cards.title: The farthest thing we ever made
cards.text: Voyager 1 launched on September 5, 1977. On August 25, 2012, it became the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space. It is the most distant human-made object, and in November 2026 it was expected to reach one light-day from Earth: a radio message takes a full day to arrive.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Voyager 1
cards.more:
Voyager 1 flew past Jupiter and Saturn, sending back the first detailed images of those giant planets and their moons, then kept going. In 2012 it crossed the heliopause, the boundary where the Sun's wind of charged particles gives way to the thin gas between the stars.

It still carries the Golden Record, a gold-plated disc of sounds, music and images from Earth, intended for anyone who might someday find it. Its power source is slowly fading, and engineers have been switching instruments off one by one to keep it talking. Even after it falls silent, it will keep drifting outward for a very, very long time.

cards.title: The giant volcano of Mars
cards.text: Olympus Mons on Mars is about 21 kilometres high, roughly two and a half times the height of Mount Everest above sea level. It is about 600 kilometres wide and covers some 300,000 square kilometres, roughly the size of Italy. It is the tallest mountain on any planet we know.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Olympus Mons
cards.more:
Olympus Mons is a shield volcano, built up by countless flows of runny lava, like the volcanoes of Hawaii but on a vastly bigger scale. Why is it so huge? Mars lacks moving tectonic plates. On Earth, plates slide over volcanic hotspots, spreading eruptions out into chains of islands. On Mars, the crust stays fixed over the hotspot, so a volcano can keep erupting in the same place until it reaches an enormous height.

Its only real rival is Rheasilvia, a central peak on the asteroid Vesta, which is roughly tied with it as the tallest mountain yet found in the solar system. Earth has nothing remotely close.

cards.title: The Sun is almost everything
cards.text: The Sun holds 99.86 percent of all the mass in the solar system. Jupiter and Saturn make up nearly 90 percent of what's left. Earth, the Moon and every other planet, moon, asteroid and comet are, by comparison, crumbs.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Solar System; Sun
cards.more:
The Sun formed about 4.6 billion years ago, when a dense region of a gas cloud collapsed. Most of the material fell to the centre; the planets assembled from the thin disc of leftovers spinning around it.

That mass powers everything. In the Sun's core, hydrogen fuses into helium, and each second more than four billion kilograms of matter are converted into energy, as described by Einstein's E = mc². Even at that rate, the Sun has used up only a tiny fraction of its mass so far. It's about halfway through its stable, hydrogen-burning life, with billions of years still to go.

cards.title: Moving the Sun to the centre
cards.text: Nicolaus Copernicus proposed that Earth is not the fixed centre of everything. In his model, Earth is one of several planets circling the Sun while spinning daily on its axis. The strange backward loops planets seem to make in our sky became simple: we watch them from a moving platform.
cards.author: Nicolaus Copernicus
cards.source: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium (1543)
cards.more:
The idea wasn't completely new; the ancient Greek astronomer Aristarchus had suggested a Sun-centred system centuries earlier. But Copernicus worked it out mathematically in detail. His book appeared in 1543, the year he died. According to a well-known story, he was handed a printed copy on his deathbed.

His model still relied on perfect circles, which kept it from matching the planets exactly. Its real power lay in its simplicity and in the questions it raised. It took Kepler's ellipses and Galileo's telescope to turn it into something no one could reasonably deny.

cards.title: Eight minutes that changed astronomy
cards.text: Johannes Kepler spent years trying to fit the orbit of Mars with circles. His best circular model missed Tycho Brahe's observations by just eight minutes of arc, about a quarter of the Moon's apparent width. Kepler refused to ignore the gap, trusted the data, and found the true shape: an ellipse.
cards.author: Johannes Kepler
cards.source: Astronomia nova (1609)
cards.more:
Tycho Brahe had spent decades making the most precise naked-eye measurements of the planets ever recorded. Eight arcminutes was larger than his observational error, and Kepler took that seriously. He wrote that those eight minutes alone would lead to the reform of all of astronomy.

They did. Kepler published his laws of planetary motion between 1609 and 1621: orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus, planets speed up when closer to the Sun, and there's a precise link between a planet's distance and its year. Decades later, Isaac Newton showed that gravity explains all three. It's a great lesson in honesty: the small discrepancy you're tempted to ignore can be the discovery.

cards.title: Where is everybody?
cards.text: Our galaxy has somewhere between 100 and 400 billion stars, many far older than the Sun, and probably at least as many planets. If even a tiny fraction produced civilisations that could travel or signal between stars, some should have spread far by now. So why haven't we seen any sign of them?
cards.source: Wikipedia: Fermi paradox; Milky Way
cards.more:
The puzzle is named after physicist Enrico Fermi. In 1950, over lunch at Los Alamos, a conversation about flying saucers moved on to other topics, and Fermi suddenly asked something like: where is everybody?

There are many possible answers, and each one says something striking. Maybe life is common but intelligence is rare. Maybe civilisations tend to destroy themselves or simply stay home. Maybe they're out there but too far apart in space and time, or communicate in ways we haven't thought to look for. Or maybe we really are alone. Every answer, if true, would be one of the most important facts we could ever learn.

cards.title: The only thing that’s truly good
cards.text: The Stoics made a bold claim: only virtue is truly good. Wisdom, justice, courage and self-control can never be misused. Money, health and status are nice to have, but they are ‘indifferents’: they can serve a good life or a bad one. What counts is how you use them.
cards.author: Zeno of Citium
cards.source: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book 7
cards.more:
Stoicism began around 300 BC, when Zeno of Citium started teaching in a painted colonnade in Athens. Its central move is to split the world into what is genuinely good (a good character), what is genuinely bad (a bad character), and everything else. The Stoics called the rest ‘indifferents’, though they admitted some are preferred: health beats sickness, and you’re allowed to pursue it.

The point isn’t to despise comfort. It’s that no outside thing can make you a good person or stop you from being one. That changes your scorecard. A missed promotion can’t fail you; acting badly to get one can. The rest of this thread builds on that foundation.

thread.title: Stoicism in 7 cards

cards.text: Of things some are in our power, and others are not. … Not in our power are the body, property, reputation, offices (magisterial power), and in a word, whatever are not our own acts.
cards.author: Epictetus
cards.source: Encheiridion, 1 (trans. George Long, 1877)
cards.more:
This is the opening line of the Encheiridion, or ‘handbook’, a short summary of Epictetus’ teaching put together by his student Arrian. Epictetus sorts everything into two piles. Your judgments, intentions and desires are yours. Your body, your money and what people think of you are, in the end, up to the world.

It sounds obvious, yet most daily stress comes from mixing up the piles: trying to control someone else’s opinion while neglecting the one thing you do steer, your response. A practical test before you start worrying: which pile does this belong in? If it isn’t yours, put your effort into the part that is.

thread.title: Stoicism in 7 cards

cards.text: Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things; for example, death is nothing terrible, for if it were it would have seemed so to Socrates…
cards.author: Epictetus
cards.source: Encheiridion, 5 (trans. George Long, 1877)
cards.more:
Once you know what’s in your power, Epictetus points at the most important item on the list: your judgments. An event arrives, then comes the story you tell about it: this is a disaster, this is an insult. Most of the suffering lives in that second step.

This isn’t a claim that pain is fake. It’s a claim that there is more room than you think between what happens and how you take it. Modern cognitive behavioural therapy grew partly out of the same insight, and its founders credited the Stoics. Next time you’re upset, try naming the judgment underneath the feeling, then ask whether it’s actually true.

thread.title: Stoicism in 7 cards

cards.text: …nothing ought to be unexpected by us. Our minds should be sent forward in advance to meet all problems, and we should consider, not what is wont to happen, but what can happen.
cards.author: Seneca
cards.source: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 91 (trans. Richard M. Gummere, 1920)
cards.more:
Seneca wrote this after a fire destroyed the city of Lyon in a single night, leaving a friend of his badly shaken. His advice became a Stoic exercise later known as premeditatio malorum: rehearsing in your mind the things that could go wrong.

It sounds gloomy, but the aim is the opposite of anxiety. If you have already pictured losing a job, a plan falling through or a friendship cooling, the real event finds you prepared instead of ambushed. And while you picture the loss, you notice how much you value what you have now. A few calm minutes of this before a big week goes a long way.

thread.title: Stoicism in 7 cards

cards.text: Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish; but wish the things which happen to be as they are, and you will have a tranquil flow of life.
cards.author: Epictetus
cards.source: Encheiridion, 8 (trans. George Long, 1877)
cards.more:
After preparing for misfortune comes the harder step: accepting what has actually happened. Epictetus isn’t telling you to stop trying. You can work hard for an outcome. But once the result is in, arguing with reality only adds a second injury to the first.

The phrase ‘tranquil flow of life’ echoes an old Stoic definition of happiness as a life that flows smoothly, like a river moving around rocks instead of fighting them. Centuries later Nietzsche praised a similar attitude as amor fati, love of fate. A modern version: when plans collapse, say ‘okay, this is what’s happening’ before you ask ‘so what now?’

thread.title: Stoicism in 7 cards

cards.title: Pull your circles closer
cards.text: Hierocles pictured each person at the centre of rings: your mind, then family, relatives, neighbours, city, country and finally all of humanity. His exercise was to keep drawing the outer rings inward. Treat cousins a little more like siblings, and strangers a little more like neighbours.
cards.author: Hierocles
cards.source: Hierocles, Elements of Ethics (fragment preserved by Stobaeus)
cards.more:
Stoicism is sometimes mistaken for a private, inward-looking calm. Hierocles, a Stoic of the 2nd century AD, shows the other half. If virtue is the only good, then justice and kindness towards others are part of the core, not optional extras. The Stoics called themselves citizens of the world.

The circles turn that big idea into a practice. You don’t have to love all of humanity in the abstract; you just have to move each ring one step closer. Call the relative you treat like an acquaintance. Learn the name of the neighbour you nod at. In this picture, inner calm and outward care are one project.

thread.title: Stoicism in 7 cards

cards.text: It was the custom of Sextius when the day was over, and he had betaken himself to rest, to inquire of his spirit: “What bad habit of yours have you cured to-day? what vice have you checked? in what respect are you better?”
cards.author: Seneca
cards.source: On Anger, Book 3.36 (trans. Aubrey Stewart, 1889)
cards.more:
This is how the whole system becomes a habit. Seneca borrowed the nightly review from the philosopher Quintus Sextius and says he does it himself: when the lamp is out, he goes over the whole day, what he said and did, hiding nothing from himself and letting himself off where he can.

It ties this thread together. Each night, ask where you confused what you control with what you don’t, which judgments made things worse, what you failed to expect, what you fought instead of accepting, and whom you could have treated better. Five quiet minutes turn Stoicism from an interesting idea into a practice. Seneca adds that the sleep afterwards is sweeter.

thread.title: Stoicism in 7 cards

cards.text: Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busybody, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial. All these things happen to them by reason of their ignorance of what is good and evil.
cards.author: Marcus Aurelius
cards.source: Meditations, Book 2.1 (trans. George Long, 1862)
cards.more:
Marcus Aurelius was the most powerful man in the world, and this is how he prepared for a workday. It isn’t cynicism. The passage goes on: these people are his kin, and we are made for cooperation like feet, hands and eyelids, so he can neither be harmed by them nor hate them.

Two ideas sit side by side here. Expect friction, so it doesn’t ambush you. And remember that people who behave badly usually don’t see what’s good, which makes them more to be pitied than hated. Try it before a tough meeting or a family dinner: name what might annoy you, then decide in advance how you want to respond.

cards.text: No longer talk at all about the kind of man that a good man ought to be, but be such.
cards.author: Marcus Aurelius
cards.source: Meditations, Book 10.16 (trans. George Long, 1862)
cards.more:
By Book 10 of the Meditations, Marcus sounds impatient with himself. He had studied with the best teachers, absorbed the arguments and could describe the good life in detail. This line is him cutting off his own stalling.

There’s a familiar trap in self-improvement: reading about it, planning it, discussing it, everything except doing it. Talking about virtue can even feel like progress, which makes it a comfortable place to hide. Marcus’s fix is blunt. Pick the one quality you keep describing, whether patience, honesty or focus, and practise it once today in a small, real situation. The theory can wait.

cards.text: Nothing, Lucilius, is ours, except time. We were entrusted by nature with the ownership of this single thing, so fleeting and slippery that anyone who will can oust us from possession.
cards.author: Seneca
cards.source: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 1 (trans. Richard M. Gummere, 1917)
cards.more:
This comes from the first of Seneca’s 124 surviving letters to his friend Lucilius, written in the last years of his life. He points out how carefully we guard money and possessions while letting others spend our hours freely, and how nobody feels in debt for having taken someone’s time.

The letters were Seneca’s way of teaching philosophy as a conversation between friends, and this one feels very modern. Notifications, meetings and endless feeds all ‘oust us from possession’. Try auditing one day the way you would a budget: where did the hours actually go, and who decided?

cards.text: There are more things, Lucilius, likely to frighten us than there are to crush us; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality.
cards.author: Seneca
cards.source: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 13 (trans. Richard M. Gummere, 1917)
cards.more:
Seneca wrote this to a friend bracing for trouble. His point is simple: many of the disasters we dread never arrive, and the ones that do rarely look the way we pictured them. Meanwhile, the worrying is already real suffering.

In the same letter he sorts our fears into three kinds: some things torment us more than they should, some before they should, and some that never should at all. It’s a handy checklist. When your mind races ahead, ask which kind this is, and what you actually know right now. Then deal with that, and let tomorrow’s version wait until tomorrow.

cards.text: Lead me, O Zeus, and thou O Destiny, The way that I am bid by you to go: To follow I am ready. If I choose not, I make myself a wretch, and still must follow.
cards.author: Cleanthes
cards.source: Quoted in Epictetus, Encheiridion, 52 (trans. George Long, 1877)
cards.more:
Cleanthes was Zeno’s successor as head of the Stoic school, a former boxer who paid for his studies by carrying water at night. His lines were so loved that Epictetus used them near the end of his handbook, and Seneca later turned them into Latin with an extra line: fate leads the willing and drags the unwilling.

The idea is that the road goes where it goes either way. What you choose is the walk: with your head up, or kicking and resisting the whole time. You can’t always pick what happens to you. You can decide whether you meet it gracefully or wear yourself out fighting it.

cards.title: The view from above
cards.text: Marcus Aurelius had a habit of zooming out. Picture the whole earth from high above: countless people being born, arguing, celebrating, dying. Now find your current problem in that picture. Most of what feels huge shrinks to its real size, and so does the hunger for praise.
cards.author: Marcus Aurelius
cards.source: Meditations, Book 9.30 (trans. George Long, 1862)
cards.more:
Marcus returns to this image again and again in the Meditations: look down from above on the crowds of humanity, their voyages, feasts and quarrels, and on the people of the past and future who will never know your name. The historian Pierre Hadot called it ‘the view from above’.

It isn’t meant to make you feel worthless. It’s meant to restore proportion. An awkward email, a rival’s success, a bad review: from high enough up, they’re tiny, while the way you treat people stays important. Try it when something is eating at you. Zoom out to the street, the city, the planet, then come back and act.

cards.title: Philosophy is for women too
cards.text: In first-century Rome, Musonius Rufus argued that women should study philosophy just as men do. Women, he said, have the same reason, the same senses and the same natural pull toward virtue. If philosophy teaches you how to live well, nobody should be shut out of it.
cards.author: Musonius Rufus
cards.source: Lectures, 3: That Women Too Should Study Philosophy
cards.more:
Musonius Rufus was one of the most respected teachers in imperial Rome and the teacher of Epictetus. His lectures survive in notes taken down by his students. Two of them argue that women should study philosophy and that daughters deserve the same education as sons, a striking position for his time.

His reasoning is very Stoic. If the good life depends on reason and character, not on status or the body, then the capacity for it is shared by everyone. He also insisted that philosophy should be practised, not just discussed. The lesson still lands: when a tradition says a good life is for everyone, check who it actually invites in.

cards.title: The obstacle is the way
cards.text: Ryan Holiday built a whole book on one line from Marcus Aurelius: the mind can turn whatever blocks it into material to work with. A setback becomes a chance to practise patience, creativity or courage. You don’t get around obstacles to reach the good life; you use them.
cards.author: Ryan Holiday
cards.source: The Obstacle Is the Way (2014), drawing on Meditations, Book 5.20
cards.more:
In Book 5 of the Meditations, Marcus notes that other people can block his actions, but not his attitude. The mind converts each hindrance into an aid, so the obstacle on the road helps us along the road. Holiday’s 2014 book retells this idea through stories of athletes, generals and entrepreneurs, and it helped spark the modern Stoicism revival.

The practical move is a question: what does this obstacle let me practise? A cancelled plan gives you time. A harsh critic gives you a chance at patience, or useful feedback. Not every problem has a silver lining, but nearly every one offers something to train.

cards.title: Philosophy as daily exercise
cards.text: The historian Pierre Hadot argued that ancient philosophy wasn’t mainly a set of theories. It was a training programme for the mind. Stoic writings are full of exercises, repeated reminders and rehearsals, meant to change how you see the world, not just what you believe.
cards.author: Pierre Hadot
cards.source: Philosophy as a Way of Life (1995)
cards.more:
Hadot, a French scholar of ancient thought, noticed something odd about the Meditations. Marcus repeats himself constantly. Hadot’s explanation: these weren’t essays for readers but spiritual exercises, notes Marcus wrote to reshape his own habits of thought, the way an athlete repeats drills.

That reframes what reading philosophy is for. Understanding an idea once is easy; living by it takes rehearsal. If a Stoic line hits home, treat it like a workout. Write it down, return to it daily and test it against real situations. The point isn’t to collect insights. It’s to become, slowly, someone who acts on them without having to think.

cards.title: Stoicism started with a shipwreck
cards.text: Zeno of Citium was a wealthy merchant until he survived a shipwreck on the way to Athens. In a bookshop there he read about Socrates and asked where to find men like that. Around 301 BC he began teaching in the Stoa Poikile, the Painted Porch, which gave Stoicism its name.
cards.author: Zeno of Citium
cards.source: Wikipedia: Zeno of Citium
cards.more:
The story comes from Diogenes Laërtius, an ancient biographer, so some details may be embellished, but it’s the account Zeno’s followers told. The bookseller reportedly pointed to Crates the Cynic, who happened to be walking by, and Zeno became his student before founding his own school.

His students were first called Zenonians, but the name that stuck came from the place: a colonnade decorated with paintings in the Athenian marketplace. ‘Stoic’ just means ‘porch people’. Fitting for a philosophy built on the idea that losing your fortune at sea doesn’t have to be the end of a good life. Sometimes it’s the start of one.

cards.title: Meditations was never meant for us
cards.text: Marcus Aurelius wrote the Meditations in Greek, as private notes to himself, without any plan to publish. The work had no official title; one old manuscript calls it ‘to himself’. Parts were written on military campaigns along the Danube.
cards.author: Marcus Aurelius
cards.source: Wikipedia: Meditations
cards.more:
Marcus was Roman emperor from 161 to 180 AD, and he wrote in Greek, the language of philosophy for educated Romans. Notes in the text place the first book among the Quadi, a tribe he was fighting near the River Hron in modern Slovakia, and the second at Carnuntum, a military base on the Danube.

Knowing this changes how the book reads. It isn’t a guru lecturing you. It’s a tired, busy man reminding himself, again and again, how he wants to behave. That makes it one of the oldest surviving examples of journaling as self-help, and a good argument for keeping your own notebook, even if nobody else ever reads it.

cards.title: Epictetus in a prison camp
cards.text: In 1965, US pilot James Stockdale was shot down over North Vietnam and held as a prisoner of war for more than seven years. He later credited the teachings of Epictetus, a philosopher born into slavery, with giving him the strength to get through it.
cards.author: James Stockdale
cards.source: Wikipedia: James Stockdale
cards.more:
Stockdale was the most senior naval officer held captive in Hanoi, in the prison Americans called the Hanoi Hilton. He received the Medal of Honor in 1976 for his leadership as a prisoner, and later spent years at Stanford’s Hoover Institution writing and lecturing on Stoicism.

He later wrote an essay titled Courage Under Fire: Testing Epictetus’s Doctrines in a Laboratory of Human Behavior. The lesson he drew is the dichotomy of control at its most extreme: his captors could control his body and circumstances, but not his judgments or his will. Epictetus, a former slave, had taught exactly that.

cards.title: What would you still have?
cards.text: Imagine a fire takes everything tonight: house, things, savings, the lot. Make a list of what you would still have. Is that list where you spend most of your attention?
cards.author: Seneca
cards.source: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 9 (trans. Richard M. Gummere, 1917)
cards.more:
Seneca tells the story of Stilbo, a philosopher whose city was captured and whose wife and children were lost. When the conquering general Demetrius asked whether he had lost anything, Stilbo answered: ‘I have all my goods with me!’ He meant his character, his judgment and his values, the things no army could carry off.

The Stoics didn’t pretend losses don’t hurt. But the thought experiment shows what you actually depend on. If most of your worry goes to things that could burn, and little to the things that couldn’t, it may be worth shifting the balance a little.

cards.title: Have you done it too?
cards.text: Think of the last person who really annoyed you. Now be honest: have you ever done something similar, or wanted to? How does that change the anger?
cards.author: Marcus Aurelius
cards.source: Meditations, Book 11.18 (trans. George Long, 1862)
cards.more:
In Book 11, Marcus lists ways to cool down when someone offends him. One of them: consider that you also do many things wrong, and that you are a person like others. Even when you avoid a particular fault, he says, you often have the disposition for it and are held back only by caution or concern for your reputation.

This isn’t about excusing bad behaviour. It’s about seeing it clearly. Most anger quietly assumes that the other person is a different kind of creature from you. Remembering your own lapses brings them back to human size, and makes a calm, fair response much easier to find.

cards.title: The judge who found English's lost cousins
cards.text: In 1786 William Jones, a British judge in Calcutta, told the Asiatic Society that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin were too alike to be a coincidence. They must have sprung from a common source that no longer existed, and Gothic, Celtic and Persian probably did too. That lost source is now called Proto-Indo-European.
cards.source: William Jones, Third Anniversary Discourse to the Asiatic Society (1786); Wikipedia, William Jones (philologist)
cards.more:
Jones wasn't the first to notice the resemblances, and he got some things wrong, lumping in languages like Egyptian and Japanese. But his lecture caught the moment and launched comparative linguistics.

The family he pointed to now includes most languages of Europe, Iran and northern India, from Hindi to Welsh to English. Nearly half the world's people speak one natively.

No one ever wrote Proto-Indo-European down. It was spoken roughly five or six thousand years ago, and everything we know about it has been reconstructed by comparing its descendants. This thread follows one branch of that family all the way to the English you're reading now.

thread.title: How English became English (7 cards)

cards.title: Why father sounds like pater
cards.text: Latin pater, English father. Latin pes, ped-, English foot. Latin tres, English three. The pattern is regular: where Latin and Greek kept an old p or t, the Germanic languages shifted it to f or th. Rasmus Rask spotted it, and Jacob Grimm, of the fairy tales, laid it out in 1822.
cards.source: Jacob Grimm, Deutsche Grammatik (1822); Wikipedia, Grimm's law
cards.more:
Grimm's law describes a set of consonant changes that happened in the ancestor of the Germanic languages, probably in the first millennium BC. P became f, t became th, k became h, and other stops shifted in step.

It explains pairs that look unrelated at first: Latin cornu and English horn, Latin piscis and English fish. It's also why English often has two versions of one root, a native word and a later borrowing from Latin: father and paternal, foot and pedal.

The big lesson was that sound change isn't random. It follows rules, which turned the study of language into something closer to a science.

thread.title: How English became English (7 cards)

cards.title: English arrived by boat
cards.text: English was not born in England. It came over with Germanic settlers, the Angles, Saxons and their neighbours, who crossed the North Sea in the mid-5th century. Their language, Old English, is so different from ours that the opening of Beowulf, which begins Hwaet!, needs a translation.
cards.source: Wikipedia, Old English; Beowulf
cards.more:
The name itself is a souvenir of the migration: English comes from the Angles, and England was once Englaland, land of the Angles.

The only manuscript of Beowulf was copied around 975 to 1025 and nearly burned in a library fire in 1731. Its language had grammatical endings much like modern German, and letters we have since lost, such as thorn and ash.

The Celtic languages already spoken in Britain left surprisingly few words in English, mostly place and river names, like Thames and Avon. What would really reshape English was the next wave of invaders, who spoke a close cousin of Old English.

thread.title: How English became English (7 cards)

cards.title: The Vikings gave us they
cards.text: Viking settlers in England left behind some of the most basic words we have: they, them and their, plus egg, knife, skin and sky, which in Old Norse meant cloud. Window comes from vindauga, literally wind-eye.
cards.source: Wikipedia, List of English words of Old Norse origin (citing the Online Etymology Dictionary)
cards.more:
Norse speakers settled across northern and eastern England from the 9th to the 11th centuries, in the region called the Danelaw. Old English and Old Norse were close enough that neighbours could probably get the gist of each other.

Borrowing nouns is common when cultures meet. Borrowing pronouns is rare, and it shows how deeply the two populations blended in daily life.

Some scholars think this mixing also helped English shed many of its grammatical endings. When two related languages share roots but differ in endings, speakers tend to drop the endings and lean on word order instead. Then, in 1066, a very different set of invaders arrived.

thread.title: How English became English (7 cards)

cards.text: And swine is good Saxon... and pork, I think, is good Norman-French; and so when the brute lives, and is in the charge of a Saxon slave, she goes by her Saxon name; but becomes a Norman, and is called pork, when she is carried to the Castle-hall to feast among the nobles...
cards.author: Walter Scott
cards.source: Ivanhoe, ch. 1 (1819)
cards.more:
Wamba the jester is explaining to Gurth the swineherd how the Norman Conquest of 1066 split their language. The animals tended by English peasants kept their Old English names: swine, cow, sheep, calf. The meat served to the French-speaking lords took French names: pork, beef, mutton, veal.

Scott was a novelist, not a linguist, and the real story is messier, but the pattern is real and it runs through English. Plain, everyday words tend to be Germanic. Fancier words of law, government and food often came through French: begin versus commence, ask versus inquire.

For about three centuries, the people running England spoke French.

thread.title: How English became English (7 cards)

cards.title: Why English spelling looks so wrong
cards.text: Between about 1400 and 1700, the long vowels of English moved. Bite was once said roughly like beet, and house roughly like hoose. Spelling had started settling down around the same time, partly thanks to printers, so we're still writing many words the way they sounded before the Great Vowel Shift.
cards.source: Wikipedia, Great Vowel Shift
cards.more:
This is the main reason English vowel letters behave so strangely compared with Spanish, Italian or German, where a written i still sounds like ee. Chaucer, writing in the late 1300s, would have pronounced name with a vowel like the a in father.

Nobody fully knows why the shift happened. Theories include the social mixing after the Black Death and the rise of London as a centre that blended regional accents.
